description: An SOP written from memory usually documents the official story. A process map built from observation reveals the real work, hidden handoffs, workarounds, delays, and decisions the procedure must control.
html:
An SOP written from memory usually documents the official story. A process map built from observation reveals the real work, hidden handoffs, workarounds, delays, and decisions the procedure must control.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S06
Audience
Process owners, tourism operations managers, quality teams, SOP writers, and supervisors
Practical tool
As-Is/To-Be Tourism Process Mapping Worksheet
Illustrative context
Hotel pickup and airport-transfer operations

The danger of starting with a template

An operations manager asks a supervisor to write the hotel-pickup SOP. The supervisor opens a standard template and describes the process:

  1. The guide reaches the hotel.
  2. The guide meets the guests.
  3. The guests board the vehicle.
  4. The driver departs on time.

The procedure is clean and almost useless.

It does not show how the final guest list reaches the guide, how hotel zones affect sequence, who verifies a changed pickup time, how accessibility or child-seat needs reach Transport, what happens when a coach serves several hotels, how a missing guest is handled, who may release the vehicle, how the dispatcher knows the coach has departed, or what evidence closes the service.

The problem is not poor writing. The problem is that writing began before discovery.

ISO’s process-approach guidance emphasizes understanding connected activities, inputs, outputs, controls, measures, and risks. A procedure should be built on that understanding. It should not be used to discover the process while simultaneously declaring the process approved.

The operating rule is simple:

Map what happens, test what should happen, then write how it will be controlled.

The process people describe is rarely the whole process

Managers, supervisors, and employees see different parts of the same work.

A manager may describe the approved workflow. A dispatcher describes the live coordination. A guide describes guest behavior and hotel conditions. A driver describes loading and route constraints. Reservations describes booking changes. Finance describes evidence and supplier reconciliation. The guest experiences the gaps between all of them.

No single interview gives the complete picture.

The real process may also include invisible work:

  • checking several messages to find the latest time;
  • calling a colleague because the system field is unclear;
  • rewriting a manifest for the guide;
  • keeping a personal list of reliable suppliers;
  • using a screenshot when connectivity is weak;
  • asking a hotel desk to find a missing guest;
  • delaying system closure until a client answers; and
  • making an unofficial decision because the authority path is too slow.

Some workarounds are unsafe or inconsistent. Others are intelligent responses to a design gap. The mapping team must understand why the workaround exists before removing it.

As-Is and To-Be: two different maps

The As-Is map

The As-Is map represents the current process as it is actually performed. Its purpose is not to blame employees or make the company look disorganized. It establishes evidence for improvement.

The As-Is map should show:

  • actual triggers and end points;
  • real information sources;
  • actual roles and suppliers;
  • duplicate checks and rework;
  • waiting and queues;
  • informal handoffs;
  • failure points and workarounds;
  • guest touchpoints;
  • records actually created; and
  • differences by shift, client, market, or service type.

Do not clean the map during discovery. If the team draws what it wishes occurred, the later SOP will preserve the wrong assumptions.

The To-Be map

The To-Be map represents the approved future process after the team has evaluated value, risk, customer needs, authority, technology, competence, and feasibility.

It should remove unnecessary complexity while retaining necessary controls. It should define a clear source of truth, ownership, handoff, exception route, evidence, and measurement.

The To-Be process is not automatically valid because it looks simpler. It must be tested. Removing a verification step may reduce waiting but increase the risk of sending the wrong vehicle. Automating a message may improve speed but create a privacy or accuracy risk. Centralizing approvals may improve cost control but delay service recovery.

Define the process before drawing it

Complete a one-page definition first.

Purpose

What result must the process produce for the guest, client, and company?

Example: collect confirmed guests from their assigned hotels and deliver them to the event venue according to the approved movement plan, with appropriate guest care, timing, accessibility, communication, and evidence.

Trigger

What event starts the process?

“The guide arrives at the hotel” is too late. The process may start when the approved movement plan is released or when the final pickup manifest becomes effective.

End point

When is the process closed?

Vehicle departure is not necessarily closure. The operation may need venue arrival confirmation, missing-guest disposition, completed counts, incident status, and system update.

Inputs and outputs

Inputs may include guest list, hotel, pickup window, destination, vehicle, accessibility, client instructions, contact details, signage, and authority rules.

Outputs may include guests delivered, exceptions resolved or escalated, records completed, client status updated, and service ready for reconciliation.

Scope and variations

Does the map cover private transfers, shared pickups, MICE coaches, cruise movements, VIPs, children, accessible services, or after-hours work? One map may not fit every variation.

Collect evidence, not only opinions

Observe the work

Watch the process at the point of delivery. Observe a dispatch shift, hotel departure, airport arrival, or tour-file handover. Record sequence, waiting, questions, corrections, system use, and communication.

Observation should be ethical and proportionate. Protect guest and employee privacy. Do not record personal information unnecessarily. Explain the improvement purpose and avoid turning mapping into covert performance surveillance.

Review records

Examine actual manifests, handover messages, dispatch logs, incident forms, complaint records, supplier confirmations, and change histories. Records show variation that interviews may forget.

Ask:

  • Which fields are commonly missing?
  • How many versions circulate?
  • Where are changes recorded?
  • Which exceptions recur?
  • Which evidence is incomplete?
  • Which work is performed outside the approved system?

Interview across the handoffs

Interview the person who supplies the input, the person who performs the work, and the person who receives the output.

Use questions such as:

  • What must be true before you can begin?
  • Where do you obtain the information?
  • How do you know it is current?
  • What do you verify?
  • What normally goes wrong?
  • What do you do when it goes wrong?
  • Which decision requires approval?
  • What do you produce, and who receives it?
  • How does the next person know the handoff is complete?
  • What would make the work safer or easier?

Walk one real case end to end

Select a completed service and reconstruct the journey from booking to closure. Use timestamps and records. A real case exposes transitions that generic discussion misses.

Build the As-Is map

Start with five to ten stages

For hotel pickup:

Release plan → validate manifest → assign team/vehicle → confirm readiness → position at hotel → call and board guests → release vehicle → arrive at venue → close movement.

Agree on the boundary before adding detail.

Add swimlanes

Possible lanes:

  • Client/Sales;
  • Reservations;
  • Operations/Dispatch;
  • Hotel Representative or Guide;
  • Driver/Transport Supplier;
  • Hotel;
  • Venue Team; and
  • Guest.

Include systems as lanes only when system responsibility or automation matters. Otherwise annotate the activity.

Add decisions and exceptions

Examples:

  • Is the manifest complete?
  • Has the vehicle confirmed readiness?
  • Is the hotel loading point available?
  • Are all expected guests present?
  • Has the waiting threshold been reached?
  • Is the guide authorized to release the coach?
  • Has the venue accepted arrival?

Each decision needs clear outcomes. “Escalate if necessary” is not a branch.

Add information and evidence

Show the manifest, movement plan, briefing, vehicle confirmation, guest count, departure status, incident record, and completion update.

The Fleet Control Tower illustrates the value of one operating picture. The map should identify where that picture receives and validates information.

Add guest experience

Mark what the guest sees and feels: message before pickup, signage, staff visibility, waiting, boarding clarity, luggage support, updates during delay, accessibility, and arrival guidance.

This layer connects process efficiency with service quality.

Analyze the map before designing the future

Handoff risk

Look for information that changes owner without confirmation. A departure time sent in email but not updated in the manifest is a classic control gap.

Waiting

Identify where people or vehicles wait for information, approval, guests, loading space, or another supplier. Not all waiting is waste; some is a deliberate buffer. Distinguish protective capacity from unmanaged delay.

Rework

Find activities repeated because the original input was incomplete or untrusted. Multiple teams may rebuild the same guest list because no source is reliable.

Overprocessing

Identify approvals or reports that do not change a decision or satisfy a real requirement. Remove them carefully; a control may have a purpose that is not visible to the person performing it.

Failure demand

Separate normal value-creating work from work generated by previous errors: clarification calls, repeated confirmations, corrected tickets, new manifests, complaint handling, and supplier disputes.

Authority gaps

Find decisions employees face without clear limits: release a coach, change a vehicle, add waiting, split a group, contact a VIP, or incur recovery cost.

Accessibility and inclusion gaps

Check whether accessibility needs are captured, confirmed, handed over, and delivered across the complete journey. ISO 21902 addresses stakeholders across the tourism supply chain, including tour operators, transport, MICE, contractors, and suppliers. A single “wheelchair” field is not a complete accessible-service process.

Evidence gaps

Ask whether the process creates factual, proportionate records at the right moment. If a supervisor cannot reconstruct what happened without calling several people, the evidence design is weak.

Design the To-Be process

Begin with the intended outcome

Do not begin by adding technology. Define the guest and business result, then select the simplest controls that can reliably deliver it.

Establish one source of truth

Name the system or controlled document that owns critical information. Define change permission, timestamp, notification, and fallback.

Design the handoff contract

For each handoff, define sender, receiver, required information, timing, acceptance, exception, and evidence.

Example:

Reservations releases the final movement manifest to Operations by the agreed cutoff. Operations confirms acceptance or returns identified gaps within the response window. Changes after cutoff follow the late-change path and create an alert to affected roles.

Put decisions with the right role

Move routine decisions to the role closest to the work within approved limits. Escalate high-consequence or cross-functional decisions. This reduces delay without losing governance.

Design normal and exceptional paths together

Test at least three scenarios:

  • expected operation;
  • common exception; and
  • high-impact disruption.

For hotel pickup, test a complete group, one missing guest, and an unready vehicle or inaccessible loading point.

Define evidence and measures

Decide what must be recorded and how performance will be reviewed. Avoid collecting fields that no one owns or uses.

Assign implementation work

The To-Be map may require system changes, supplier agreements, training, new tools, data cleanup, or authority approval. The SOP cannot compensate for an unimplemented dependency.

Validate before writing

Tabletop walkthrough

Give participants a scenario and walk the map step by step. Ask who acts, what information they use, what decision they make, and what evidence they produce.

Field pilot

Use the future process on a controlled service. Observe usability, timing, workload, guest communication, and system behavior. A pilot should have defined success criteria and a rollback or fallback plan.

Exception simulation

Simulate a flight change, missing guest, vehicle failure, system outage, or late client amendment. How to Conduct an Operational Risk Assessment Before Writing an SOP helps select scenarios.

User acceptance

The process owner approves the design, but users must confirm that the process is understandable and feasible. Acceptance does not mean every personal preference is adopted. It means concerns are evaluated and decisions recorded.

Convert the validated map into documents

Only now should the team decide what documentation is required.

  • process definition and map for the end-to-end flow;
  • SOP for controlled execution;
  • work instructions for detailed tasks;
  • checklist for critical readiness or confirmation;
  • form for structured evidence;
  • template for recurring communication;
  • authority matrix for decisions; and
  • KPI definitions for performance.

Use the map to maintain traceability. Each procedure step should correspond to an activity, decision, control, or handoff. Each major process risk should have a designed treatment or escalation. Each required record should support a defined purpose.

Common mistakes

Mapping the ideal process as the current process

The team loses the evidence needed to understand gaps and adoption difficulty.

Blaming the person shown in the box

The map describes system behavior. A repeated manual correction may be caused by poor input design, workload, or system limitations.

Automating a broken process

Automation makes the wrong path faster and harder to see. Simplify and validate first.

Designing without suppliers

Transport, hotels, venues, attractions, guides, and other partners may perform critical steps. Invite them or validate assumptions with them.

Using one workshop as proof

A workshop captures opinions. Combine observation, records, real cases, and pilot evidence.

Writing the SOP while decisions remain open

Writers fill gaps with assumptions. Record unresolved issues and assign owners before approval.

Practical tool: As-Is/To-Be Tourism Process Mapping Worksheet

Worksheet fieldAs-Is evidenceTo-Be decision
Purpose and boundaryWhat actually triggers and closes work?What should trigger and close the approved process?
InputsWhat arrives, from whom, in what condition?What is required, by when, and how accepted?
Roles and suppliersWho actually participates?Who should be responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed?
ActivitiesWhat work is really performed?Which activities add value or control risk?
HandoffsHow does information/responsibility move?What handoff contract will apply?
Waiting and reworkWhere and why do delays/corrections occur?What can be removed, buffered, or controlled?
DecisionsWho decides today, formally or informally?Which role and authority limit should apply?
Guest experienceWhat does the guest see, need, and feel?What experience and communication should be designed?
ExceptionsWhich variations recur?What trigger, response, escalation, and fallback will apply?
Systems/documentsWhat sources and workarounds are used?What source of truth and controlled tools are required?
Records/measuresWhat evidence and data exist?What evidence and indicators will support control and learning?
ImplementationWhat prevents the current process from changing?What system, supplier, training, authority, or resource work is required?

Final perspective

The first draft of an SOP should not be the first time the organization sees its process.

Mapping creates the shared evidence needed to design the right method. It reveals where value moves, where information weakens, where the guest waits, where employees improvise, where suppliers influence delivery, and where authority is missing.

When the As-Is process is understood and the To-Be process is tested, the SOP writer is no longer guessing. The writer is converting an approved operating design into controlled, usable information.

That is the difference between documenting activity and engineering reliable service.

Continue the series

  • Procedures, Processes and Process Maps: What Is the Difference?
  • How to Conduct an Operational Risk Assessment Before Writing an SOP
  • How to Apply Customer Journey Mapping to SOP Design

  • Existing project: InfraCluster

Sources and further reading

  • ISO, The process approach in ISO 9001:2015
  • ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group, Guidance on processes
  • ISO 10013:2021, Guidance for documented information
  • ASQ, SIPOC diagram
  • ASQ, Process SIPOC template
  • ISO 21902:2021, Accessible tourism for all

Editorial note: Observation, records, and examples must be handled with appropriate privacy, employment, contractual, and information-security controls. The method is practical guidance, not a mandated audit or certification method.

description: A practical way to set process boundaries, expose missing inputs, and agree what a tourism service must deliver before anyone writes the detailed SOP.
html:
A practical way to set process boundaries, expose missing inputs, and agree what a tourism service must deliver before anyone writes the detailed SOP.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S07
Audience
DMC managers, process owners, quality teams, and supervisors preparing or improving tourism SOPs
Practical tool
Tourism SIPOC canvas with requirement and risk prompts
Running example
An airport transfer from confirmed booking to verified hotel drop-off

The operating problem

SIPOC is valuable because it creates a disciplined one-page conversation about suppliers, inputs, the high-level process, outputs, and customers. It is not a replacement for observation, a process map, or an SOP. Tourism work makes this discipline unusually important. A single service may join Sales, Reservations, Operations, a hotel, an airport team, a transport partner, a guide, a client, and the guest. Information changes while the service is live, and the person who notices a problem may not hold the authority to change cost, timing, supplier, or customer promise. The document therefore has to work as an operating interface, not simply as well-written office content. The starting point is the broader system described in the operating-system overview. That system separates governance, execution, evidence, measurement, and improvement. The present article focuses on one controlled component, while the document-type comparison explains why an SOP, work instruction, checklist, form, template, and record should not be asked to perform the same job. This is a practical management model, not a universal template imposed by ISO or a substitute for applicable law, contract terms, safety requirements, privacy advice, or emergency arrangements. An organization should tailor the depth, approval, terminology, and retained evidence to its services, risk, size, jurisdiction, technology, and competence. Approval should therefore be evidence-led. Reviewers should see the mapped work, representative records, relevant risk and guest requirements, user-test observations, and unresolved issues—not only the polished draft. That evidence makes the approval decision explainable and gives the owner a baseline for measuring whether the released control improves real performance.

The distinctions that prevent document failure

A supplier is any role, system, or organization that provides an input. In tourism, Sales, an airline feed, a hotel, a transport partner, or the guest may all be suppliers within the same process. An input is something the process consumes or relies on: a confirmed service order, flight details, guest contacts, vehicle capacity, access instructions, or an approved rate. Naming a department instead of the information it supplies hides the real dependency. An output is a verifiable result, not merely an activity. A dispatched vehicle is an activity milestone; a guest transferred to the correct hotel, with completion status and exceptions recorded, is an operational output. The customer may be external or internal. The traveller receives the experience, while Finance, Sales, the next shift, and the client account team may depend on accurate completion evidence.

Practical tool: Tourism SIPOC canvas with requirement and risk prompts

The following canvas is designed for a working session, not decorative inclusion in a manual. Complete it using a real service and current records. Every answer should be specific enough for another role to validate.

ElementControl questionTourism example
SupplierWho provides something essential?Airline feed, client, Sales, hotel, transport partner
InputWhat must be correct and available?Service order, manifest, flight status, contacts, access notes
ProcessWhat five to seven stages transform the inputs?Validate, assign, brief, monitor, meet, transfer, close
OutputWhat result and evidence must exist?Correct drop-off, timestamps, status, exception record
CustomerWho receives or depends on the output?Guest, client, hotel, Finance, next shift
RequirementHow will good be recognized?Timeliness, accuracy, safety, accessibility, communication

The table is intentionally compact. Supporting detail should live in the appropriate controlled document or system rather than expanding one tool until it becomes impossible to use. During review, mark assumptions, unresolved authority, weak inputs, and missing evidence separately; do not convert them into confident statements merely to finish the template.

A professional design workflow

1. Fix the boundary

Name one trigger and one completion point. ‘Airport operations’ is too broad; ‘confirmed arrival transfer received’ to ‘guest and baggage delivered and service closed’ can be tested and mapped.

2. Start with outputs and customers

Ask what must be true at the end and who needs that result. This resists the common tendency to reproduce the current department chart instead of designing around service value.

3. Identify inputs and their specifications

Record not just ‘manifest’ but the minimum usable standard: current version, traveller names, flight number, arrival date, contact method, mobility or assistance notes where lawfully collected, and an owner for corrections.

4. Write only the high-level process

Use five to seven verb-led stages. If the team is debating individual clicks or message wording, capture those issues for the process map, work instruction, checklist, or template rather than overloading the SIPOC.

5. Test handoffs and failure exposure

For every supplier-input pair, ask how the team knows the input has arrived, whether it is complete, and what happens if it is late or contradictory. These questions feed the risk assessment and exception design.

6. Validate with the people doing the work

Run a short workshop with Sales, Reservations, Operations, the field team, and at least one partner-facing role. Resolve language differences and record remaining assumptions before the SIPOC is approved. After completing the workflow, test the connected design during an airport transfer from confirmed booking to verified hotel drop-off. Ask users to work from the draft and approved tools without whispered instructions. Any dependency on a particular manager's memory should be recorded, owned, and resolved through the correct control—document, system, authority, contract, resource, or competence—before release.

Running example: An airport transfer from confirmed booking to verified hotel drop-off

Before the workshop

The process owner brings three recent arrival files: one normal service, one changed flight, and one no-show. Actual records prevent the discussion becoming a memory contest.

During scoping

The group decides that supplier contracting and post-service invoicing sit outside this SIPOC. They remain connected processes, but including them would make the operating boundary too wide for useful SOP design.

During input review

The team discovers that the driver brief contains a hotel entrance note while the guide brief does not. The missing shared input explains repeated calls on live days.

During output review

‘Transfer completed’ is split into guest delivered, baggage reconciled, completion time recorded, and any service exception linked to the job reference.

After approval

The SIPOC becomes the front-end design record. The detailed map, risk register, SOP, checklist, and form can now be checked against the same boundaries and requirements.

The scenario should be validated against the service's current risk assessment and guest journey, not treated as a perfect script. Compare it with the methods in operational risk assessment before SOP writing and customer journey mapping for SOP design. Those articles help the team check whether an internally neat design also addresses operational uncertainty and the guest's visible experience.

Common failure modes—and the design response

  • Mapping a department rather than a process. Use a recent case to show the operational consequence and identify the earliest control that could have prevented or detected it.
  • Treating every stakeholder as the customer. Trace the issue across roles and handoffs; the visible error may originate in an earlier input, authority decision, or system rule.
  • Using nouns such as ‘transport’ instead of verb-led process stages. Decide whether the remedy belongs in this document, a supporting tool, the system, the contract, resource planning, or competence development.
  • Listing software names without the information they provide. Test the proposed correction in a normal case and an exception so that solving one failure does not create another downstream.
  • Turning the sipoc into a forty-step procedure. Assign an owner and evidence for the correction, then set a date to confirm that the failure has not simply moved into an unofficial workaround.
  • Approving the canvas without front-line or partner validation. Where risk remains, record and escalate it explicitly rather than adding vague cautionary prose that no user can apply under pressure.

Implementation and control

  1. Appoint one process owner. Confirm the mandate, affected processes, and release decision so ownership does not disappear after the workshop.
  2. Time-box the first workshop. Schedule the work around live operations and include every shift, location, or partner needed to validate the design.
  3. Keep an assumptions and issue log. Keep an issue log with decision owner and due date; unresolved assumptions should never be disguised as approved instructions.
  4. Link the approved canvas to the process map and risk assessment. Define the evidence of readiness—approved content, system access, supporting tools, briefed partners, competent users, and supervisor cover.
  5. Review the sipoc after material supplier, system, or service changes. Set an early-use review and a routine review trigger, then route defects, competence gaps, and resource problems to different actions.

Implementation should be staged. Begin with a representative service, observe use, and correct design defects before large-scale release. Control the approved version through document control and version management, and use training, competency, and SOP adoption to distinguish a distribution list from genuine competence and adoption.

Measures that show whether the control works

A useful measure should help the owner decide, not simply make a dashboard look complete. Establish a definition, data source, owner, review frequency, context, and action threshold for each selected measure.

Candidate measureWhat the owner should learn
Percentage of required inputs complete at handoffWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Late-input exceptions per 100 servicesWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
First-time-right assignment rateWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
On-time meeting and drop-off rateWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Services closed with complete evidenceWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome

Do not read one indicator in isolation. A perfect completion rate alongside rising clarification calls may indicate retrospective box-ticking. A temporary increase in reported exceptions can be healthy after training if staff have begun recording issues that were previously hidden. Pair compliance, outcome, user-friction, guest, and improvement signals.

Field review before approval

Boundary

Does the document begin and end at points the team can identify, or does it absorb adjacent processes until no owner can validate it? State the trigger, completion condition, excluded work, and connected processes. Then follow one real job reference from start to finish and note every point where the draft crosses its own boundary.

Roles and authority

Can every action and decision be traced to a current role, deputy, authority level, and escalation path across shifts and partners? Compare the draft with rosters, job descriptions, delegation limits, and partner contacts. Ask the night or weekend shift who actually decides when the named manager is unavailable.

Time and sequence

Are triggers, deadlines, intervals, pause points, and handoffs measurable in the systems and working conditions actually used? Use timestamps from a normal case and a disrupted case. Replace vague timing with an observable event or controlled threshold, and confirm that the relevant system or record can capture it.

Information quality

Are required inputs current, traceable, appropriately protected, and presented in a form that the receiving role can use without reinterpretation? Trace each critical value to its source, owner, format, and latest valid version. Resolve duplicate fields and define what the receiver does when two approved-looking sources disagree.

Exceptions

Has the team tested delay, absence, conflicting information, technology failure, supplier failure, accessibility needs, and a changing guest situation? Run at least one scenario that exceeds front-line authority. Observe whether staff can recognize the trigger, stabilize the service, escalate with the right facts, communicate, and return the case to controlled closure.

Evidence

Does the record capture timely facts, source, action, authority, and outcome without unnecessary personal data, speculation, or retrospective reconstruction? Reconstruct a recent event using only retained records. Missing links reveal where the design needs a prompt, automatic timestamp, approval trace, attachment rule, or clearer close-out responsibility.

Guest experience

Does the control protect the guest's clarity, dignity, accessibility, time, and communication needs as well as the company's internal workflow? Walk through what the guest sees, hears, waits for, and must do. Check language, channel, physical access, assistance, uncertainty, and recovery rather than assuming internal compliance equals a good experience.

Usability

Can representative users perform the work on the actual device or paper format, under interruption and time pressure, without unofficial notes? Watch rather than coach. Record where users pause, scroll, search, abbreviate, take screenshots, or switch to personal tools; those behaviors are design evidence, not merely user resistance.

Partner interface

Do external providers understand the same requirement, status, contact, evidence, and change rules, including the right to raise a concern early? Ask the partner to explain the handoff in their own words and demonstrate the communication route. Resolve differences before release, especially around substitutions, delay, cost, guest contact, and retained evidence.

Learning and review

Will operational data, user feedback, complaints, audits, and change triggers lead to a controlled revision rather than a parallel workaround? Name who reviews which signals, how often, and what action threshold applies. Connect urgent correction, routine revision, refresher training, supplier action, and formal improvement to distinct governance routes.

How this article connects to the series

The most useful next readings are process mapping before SOP writing, operational risk assessment before SOP writing, the professional SOP structure. These links are conceptual rather than promotional: each one supplies a prerequisite, supporting control, or next implementation step. A reader should be able to follow the series from system design to live use and improvement without encountering a forced link in every paragraph. The portfolio already shows the operating context in From Airport Arrival to Final Farewell, The DMC Operations AI Toolkit, The Assignment Engine. Those pieces provide concrete examples of journeys, dashboards, assignments, quality tools, commercial controls, partner handoffs, or service recovery. This article extends them by explaining the management method behind reliable execution.

Manager's release checklist

  • The purpose, boundary, users, owner, and approval authority are explicit.
  • The content matches the approved process map, risk assessment, customer journey, and current systems.
  • Roles, deputies, thresholds, evidence, privacy, accessibility, supplier interfaces, and exceptions have been tested.
  • Supporting SOPs, work instructions, checklists, forms, templates, records, and training do not contradict one another.
  • Representative users have completed a normal and exception scenario in the actual work environment.
  • The release, access, version, change, retention, review, and withdrawal controls are ready before go-live.

Sources and further reading

  • ISO 10013:2021 — guidance for documented information
  • ISO 31000:2018 — risk management guidelines
  • Project Management Institute — Responsibility Assignment Matrix and RACI

Editorial note: This article provides operational and quality-management guidance for a professional portfolio. It does not provide legal, regulatory, privacy, safety, emergency, employment, or contractual advice. Apply qualified local review wherever those obligations affect the service.

description: Risk assessment should shape the procedure before the procedure is written. It identifies what could affect the objective, who may be harmed or impacted, which controls already exist, what remains uncertain, and where authority or escalation is required.
html:
Risk assessment should shape the procedure before the procedure is written. It identifies what could affect the objective, who may be harmed or impacted, which controls already exist, what remains uncertain, and where authority or escalation is required.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S08
Audience
Tourism operations managers, quality and safety teams, process owners, SOP writers, and supervisors
Practical tool
Tourism Operational Risk Register
Illustrative context
Airport arrival transfer with multiple exceptions

Why risk belongs before the first procedure step

An airport-transfer SOP says: “The representative shall meet the guest and escort the guest to the assigned vehicle.”

That sentence describes the intended path. It does not help the organization design controls for an early flight, missing baggage, wrong terminal, unlisted passenger, inaccessible vehicle, unready driver, privacy-sensitive contact detail, lost guest, payment dispute, severe congestion, or supplier failure.

If risk is considered only after drafting, the writer may add a generic sentence: “Any issue should be escalated to the supervisor.” The document appears complete while the difficult decisions remain undefined.

ISO 31000:2018 presents risk management as a structured approach that includes identifying, analyzing, evaluating, treating, monitoring, and communicating risk. IEC 31010:2019 provides guidance on selecting and applying risk-assessment techniques. Neither requires a tourism company to use one universal 5×5 matrix. The assessment must be adapted to context and decision needs.

The purpose before SOP writing is practical:

  • understand what could affect the process objective;
  • identify people and interests that could be affected;
  • evaluate existing controls and their reliability;
  • decide what additional controls are proportionate;
  • assign ownership and authority;
  • design monitoring, escalation, and fallback; and
  • carry those decisions into the process and documents.

Begin with the objective and context

Risk is meaningful only in relation to an objective.

For an airport arrival transfer, the objective might be:

Meet the confirmed guest at the designated point and deliver the guest and luggage to the correct destination within the approved service conditions, with appropriate safety, accessibility, guest care, communication, privacy, evidence, and cost control.

This statement is more useful than “complete the transfer” because it reveals dimensions that uncertainty can affect.

Define the context:

  • service type and volume;
  • destination and operating environment;
  • airport, hotel, venue, attraction, or transport interfaces;
  • guest profiles and access requirements;
  • time windows and dependencies;
  • internal and outsourced roles;
  • systems and information sources;
  • legal, regulatory, contractual, and client requirements;
  • language and communication needs;
  • season, weather, events, and demand; and
  • the company’s approved risk and authority criteria.

Do not copy a risk register from another destination or department without testing the context.

Identify stakeholders and possible consequences

Tourism risk is not limited to physical safety or financial loss. Consider effects on:

  • guests and companions;
  • employees and temporary staff;
  • drivers, guides, and other suppliers;
  • clients and travel partners;
  • hotels, venues, attractions, and authorities;
  • the public;
  • company operations, finance, information, and reputation; and
  • future guests if a systemic weakness is not corrected.

Possible consequence categories include:

  • injury or health impact;
  • loss of accessibility or dignity;
  • guest distress or abandonment;
  • missed programme or connection;
  • privacy or information exposure;
  • financial loss, unauthorized cost, refund, or dispute;
  • service delay or cancellation;
  • contractual non-performance;
  • supplier disruption;
  • staff overload or unsafe decision-making;
  • legal or regulatory exposure; and
  • reputational damage.

Severity should reflect more than immediate cost. A low-cost incident can have a serious human or trust impact.

Use several methods to identify risk

Process-map review

Walk through each activity, handoff, decision, guest touchpoint, and record. Ask what could prevent the intended result, create delay, produce wrong information, or weaken evidence.

The article Never Write an SOP Before Mapping the Process provides the As-Is/To-Be foundation.

Scenario workshop

Use realistic scenarios rather than asking, “What are the risks?”

Examples:

  • the flight arrives one hour early;
  • two flights release passengers at the same time;
  • the guest is not on the manifest;
  • a wheelchair user arrives but the assigned vehicle is not suitable;
  • the driver reports a mechanical warning;
  • baggage is missing and the group wants to leave;
  • the guest’s phone number is wrong;
  • the airport representative is absent;
  • the booking system is unavailable; and
  • the client changes the hotel during the operation.

Ask participants to explain signals, decisions, authority, communication, evidence, and recovery.

Record and trend review

Review complaints, incidents, near misses, service recoveries, supplier failures, late changes, audit findings, and employee observations. Historical absence of a recorded incident does not prove low risk; the reporting system may be weak.

Supplier and interface review

Risk often crosses organizational boundaries. Ask what the supplier receives, confirms, monitors, reports, and does when conditions change. Check whether authority and evidence are aligned between DMC and supplier.

Guest-journey review

Examine what the guest sees, understands, waits for, and can access. A process may be internally controlled but create confusion or exclusion. ISO 21902:2021 addresses accessible tourism across the supply chain, including transport, tour operators, MICE, contractors, and suppliers.

Write the risk clearly

Avoid single words such as “delay,” “weather,” or “supplier.” Use a cause-event-consequence structure.

Cause: final hotel change is communicated through email but not updated in the controlled dispatch plan.

Event: driver operates from the obsolete destination.

Consequence: guest is taken to the wrong hotel, arrival is delayed, client confidence is affected, additional cost occurs, and personal information may be shared during recovery.

This structure improves analysis. It separates the condition, event, and effect and helps the team select controls.

Evaluate existing controls before adding new ones

For each risk, identify current controls and test whether they are:

  • designed: capable of reducing the risk;
  • implemented: actually present in the operation;
  • used: understood and followed;
  • reliable: effective under realistic conditions; and
  • evidenced: able to show that the control operated.

An “SOP exists” is not proof of control effectiveness. The SOP may be obsolete, inaccessible, untrained, or bypassed. A supplier confirmation is weak if it confirms only the date and not the vehicle or accessibility requirement. A system alert is weak if no one owns the response.

Distinguish types of control:

  • prevention: validate mandatory fields before release;
  • detection: readiness dashboard identifies unconfirmed resources;
  • response: dispatcher activates backup vehicle;
  • recovery: guest receives update and alternative service;
  • evidence: timestamped authorization and completion record; and
  • learning: recurring causes enter corrective action and process review.

Analyze likelihood, consequence, and uncertainty

Many companies use a likelihood-consequence matrix. It can support prioritization if the scales are defined and the result is not treated as precise mathematics.

Define likelihood using evidence relevant to the process: frequency per service, season, supplier, route, or condition. Define consequence across the categories that matter. Consider the worst credible consequence and the more likely consequence where useful.

Also consider:

  • speed of onset;
  • duration;
  • detectability;
  • number of people affected;
  • dependency or concentration;
  • control reliability;
  • recovery capability; and
  • uncertainty or data quality.

A rare but severe event may require a tested contingency even if its matrix score is not the highest. A frequent low-level error may deserve priority because it creates cumulative cost and guest frustration.

Distinguish inherent, current, and residual risk

  • Inherent risk: exposure without the relevant controls.
  • Current risk: exposure with controls as they actually operate now.
  • Residual risk: exposure expected after the approved treatment is implemented and working.

Do not lower the residual score merely because an action is planned. The action must be implemented and its effectiveness verified.

If residual risk remains outside approved tolerance, the organization may need to avoid the activity, redesign the service, add capability, transfer part of the risk contractually where appropriate, or obtain a higher-level decision. Contractual transfer does not remove operational or moral responsibility.

Convert risk decisions into procedure design

The assessment should visibly change the process and SOP.

Risk decisionSOP/process response
Mandatory information frequently missingDefine validation, rejection/return path, cutoff, and late-change rule.
Vehicle accessibility not confirmedAdd requirement capture, supplier confirmation, readiness check, and escalation trigger.
Flight may arrive earlyDefine monitoring start, update threshold, resource readiness, and backup response.
Guest not locatedDefine search stages, contact permissions, waiting thresholds, authority, messages, and record.
Supplier fails to confirmDefine confirmation deadline, escalation, alternative sourcing, and approval.
System unavailableDefine authorized offline source, minimum information, reconciliation, and recovery.
Unauthorized recovery costDefine spending limits, approvers, evidence, and retrospective review.
Personal information exposedDefine data minimization, approved channels, access, retention, and incident response.

The risk register is not an appendix the employee never sees. It is a design input to responsibilities, controls, exceptions, forms, checklists, training, KPIs, and audits.

A worked airport-arrival example

Scenario

A family’s flight lands early. One passenger uses a wheelchair. The assigned accessible vehicle has not completed readiness confirmation. The main driver offers to use a standard vehicle to avoid delay.

Risk statement

Because live arrival changes and accessibility requirements are not connected to a verified vehicle-readiness control, the guest may be offered unsuitable transport, causing exclusion, distress, unsafe transfer, delay, complaint, and reputational or contractual impact.

Existing controls

  • accessibility field in booking;
  • supplier vehicle assignment;
  • dispatch call before movement; and
  • supervisor escalation.

Control gaps

  • accessibility field does not require supplier acceptance;
  • readiness call checks arrival time but not vehicle suitability;
  • no clear rule prevents substitution;
  • supervisor contact path is slow; and
  • no approved guest-update message exists.

Treatment

  • make access requirement a mandatory handoff field;
  • require explicit supplier confirmation of vehicle suitability;
  • add vehicle-suitability item to readiness checklist;
  • prohibit substitution unless the approved requirement remains satisfied;
  • define backup supplier and duty-manager authority;
  • prepare a respectful update and waiting-support plan; and
  • monitor accessibility-related readiness exceptions.

Procedure impact

The SOP gains a pre-assignment requirement, readiness control, exception trigger, authority rule, guest communication, record, and KPI. Training includes a scenario. Supplier review includes confirmation quality.

The assessment has shaped the system, not merely produced a score.

Build escalation from risk

Escalation should reflect consequence, urgency, authority, and capability.

Define:

  • trigger;
  • severity or category;
  • first owner;
  • response time;
  • decision authority;
  • required information;
  • guest/client communication owner;
  • fallback if the approver is unavailable;
  • evidence; and
  • closure/review.

“Contact management” is not a workable control. SOP Writing Part 4: Exception and Escalation Management develops the full model.

Connect operational risk and business continuity

Some risks affect one service; others disrupt a capability across many services. A single vehicle failure may be handled through normal contingency. A dispatch-system outage, airport closure, severe weather event, widespread supplier shortage, or communications failure may require business-continuity arrangements.

ISO 22301:2019 addresses the management system for preparing for, responding to, and recovering from disruption. The SOP writer should know when an exception exceeds the procedure and activates a broader continuity, emergency, or crisis plan.

Do not place emergency instructions into a generic operational SOP without competent specialist review. Life-safety, security, medical, legal, or authority-controlled responses require applicable expertise and local arrangements.

Monitor risks through indicators

Possible indicators include:

  • incomplete booking handovers;
  • late or changed service instructions;
  • supplier confirmations outside threshold;
  • unready resources at cutoff;
  • accessibility exceptions;
  • staff or vehicle substitutions;
  • services using offline fallback;
  • escalation response time;
  • unauthorized or retrospective approvals;
  • repeated incidents by cause; and
  • overdue risk treatments.

An indicator should lead to a decision. If management receives the number but no threshold, owner, or action exists, monitoring is decorative.

Common risk-assessment mistakes

Copying a generic list

The register contains “weather, traffic, accident, complaint” without relation to process objectives or controls.

Rating before understanding

The team debates whether likelihood is 3 or 4 before clarifying causes, consequences, and existing controls.

Treating the matrix as truth

The score hides uncertainty and human impact. Use judgement, evidence, and escalation criteria.

Listing the SOP as the treatment

The procedure may be part of the control, but implementation, competence, tools, authority, monitoring, and evidence determine effectiveness.

Ignoring positive uncertainty

Risk includes the effect of uncertainty on objectives, which can include opportunities. A better flight-data feed or supplier arrangement may enable earlier readiness and improved service, not only reduce loss.

Ignoring suppliers and guests

The assessment stays inside the office while delivery occurs across a supply chain and guest journey.

Closing actions without effectiveness review

An action is marked complete because a document changed. The next operating cycle must show whether the risk was actually reduced.

Practical tool: Tourism Operational Risk Register

FieldRequired content
Process objectiveResult the risk could affect.
Scope/contextService, location, period, people, systems, suppliers, and assumptions.
Risk statementCause → uncertain event → consequence.
Stakeholders affectedGuests, staff, suppliers, client, public, company.
Existing controlsPreventive, detective, response, recovery, evidence.
Control effectivenessDesign, implementation, use, reliability, evidence.
Current assessmentLikelihood, consequence, uncertainty, and rationale.
Treatment decisionAvoid, reduce, prepare/respond, share, accept with authority, or pursue opportunity.
Actions/owners/datesSpecific deliverables and accountable people.
Procedure impactStep, role, trigger, checklist, form, template, training, or KPI to change.
Residual assessmentExpected exposure after verified implementation.
Escalation/acceptanceAuthority required and conditions.
Monitoring/reviewIndicator, frequency, trigger, and next review.

Final perspective

The purpose of a pre-SOP risk assessment is not to predict every problem. It is to make uncertainty visible enough that the organization can design proportionate control, authority, monitoring, and recovery.

A strong procedure describes more than the normal path. It reflects the risks of the real process, the needs of the guest, the reliability of suppliers and systems, and the decisions employees face under pressure.

When risk assessment happens first, the SOP becomes a control design. When it happens last, risk becomes an appendix.
