  • ISO 31000:2018, Risk management — Guidelines
  • IEC 31010:2019, Risk management — Risk assessment techniques
  • ISO 22301:2019, Business continuity management systems
  • ISO 22313:2020, Guidance on applying ISO 22301
  • ISO 21902:2021, Accessible tourism for all
  • ISO 22483:2020, Hotels — Service requirements

Editorial note: Risk criteria, safety controls, accessibility arrangements, emergency response, privacy, and legal/contractual requirements must be validated for the organization and jurisdiction by competent people. The examples are management guidance, not a substitute for specialist assessment.

description: A process can be efficient for departments and still feel confusing, inaccessible, or uncaring to the guest. Journey mapping adds the human experience to the operating design before the SOP turns that design into routine work.
html:
A process can be efficient for departments and still feel confusing, inaccessible, or uncaring to the guest. Journey mapping adds the human experience to the operating design before the SOP turns that design into routine work.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S09
Audience
Tourism operations leaders, guest-experience teams, quality managers, product teams, and SOP writers
Practical tool
Dual-Layer Tourism Journey-to-SOP Map
Illustrative context
From pre-arrival to airport transfer, stay, disruption, departure, and post-service learning

The guest does not experience departments

A guest books through one company, receives a message from another, meets a representative wearing a third brand, travels in a supplier’s vehicle, checks into a hotel, joins an excursion, and contacts a call centre when something changes.

Internally, these may be separate contracts, departments, systems, and procedures. To the guest, they become one journey.

This creates an important risk in SOP design. Teams write procedures around internal responsibility:

  • Reservations sends confirmation.
  • Operations assigns transport.
  • The airport team meets the guest.
  • The driver completes the transfer.
  • The hotel handles check-in.

Every team may complete its step, yet the guest may still receive contradictory times, unclear meeting instructions, repeated questions, inaccessible transport, silence during delay, or a handoff in which no one appears responsible.

Customer journey mapping helps the organization see the experience across those boundaries. It does not replace process mapping. It adds a different lens: what the guest is trying to achieve, what the guest sees and feels, which information is needed, where trust increases or decreases, and how backstage operations create the visible moment.

ISO 23592:2021 describes a service-excellence model focused on outstanding customer experience. ISO/TS 24082:2021 addresses activities for designing excellent service. ISO 21902:2021 establishes requirements and recommendations for accessible tourism across the supply chain. Together, these sources reinforce a practical principle: service design must consider the complete experience, not only internal task completion.

Process map and journey map: connected but different

A process map asks:

  • What triggers the work?
  • Which inputs, activities, roles, decisions, and outputs are involved?
  • Where are the controls, records, and measures?

A journey map asks:

  • What is the guest trying to do?
  • What does the guest see, hear, receive, and understand?
  • What does the guest need physically, emotionally, informationally, and functionally?
  • Where does the guest wait, repeat information, or lose confidence?
  • Which moments matter most to trust and memory?

The maps should be connected. The guest’s need for a clear meeting point should link to the backstage process that creates, verifies, and sends the instruction. The guest’s need for accessible transport should link to requirement capture, supplier confirmation, assignment, readiness, and field delivery. The guest’s need for honest delay information should link to monitoring, authority, message templates, update frequency, and evidence.

Procedures, Processes and Process Maps: What Is the Difference? provides the process foundation.

Define the journey and the guest outcome

Avoid mapping “the tourist experience” as one enormous journey. Choose a clear scenario, segment, and boundary.

Example journey:

An international conference delegate travels from pre-arrival communication through airport meeting, transfer, hotel arrival, daily event movements, disruption, departure, and post-service feedback.

The outcome might be:

The delegate can understand and navigate each stage, receive the promised support, move safely and accessibly, know what happens next, and trust that the operating team will respond when conditions change.

Define variations that materially affect the journey:

  • first-time vs repeat visitor;
  • individual vs group;
  • guest language;
  • mobility, sensory, cognitive, or other access requirements;
  • child, older traveler, or unaccompanied participant;
  • VIP, speaker, crew, or standard delegate;
  • private vs shared transport;
  • direct booking vs B2B partner; and
  • normal vs disrupted service.

Do not use personas to stereotype nationality, age, disability, or spending level. Personas should represent relevant needs and behaviors supported by evidence.

Build the journey in stages

Before arrival

The guest needs confidence that the booking is correct and the arrival process is understandable.

Possible touchpoints:

  • confirmation;
  • itinerary or programme;
  • pickup instructions;
  • visa or entry information where within company scope;
  • accessibility and assistance confirmation;
  • emergency and after-hours contact;
  • what-to-bring guidance; and
  • change notifications.

Backstage controls include information validation, approved templates, translation review, timing, privacy, client approval, and version control.

Airport arrival

The guest needs to find the team, understand the next step, receive appropriate assistance, and know what happens if baggage or immigration takes longer.

Touchpoints include signage, representative visibility, meeting point, greeting, luggage coordination, waiting, and the route to the vehicle.

Backstage controls include flight monitoring, terminal verification, staff positioning, manifest control, guest search, baggage-delay response, accessible route/vehicle readiness, and dispatch communication.

The existing portfolio article Before the Delegate Reaches the Hotel provides a detailed operational application.

Transfer and hotel arrival

The guest needs the correct vehicle, a professional introduction, safe and comfortable movement, relevant information, and a smooth handoff to the hotel.

Backstage controls include vehicle/driver/guide assignment, loading, luggage count, child-seat or accessibility checks, route monitoring, hotel approach, arrival status, and completion evidence.

Experience or event delivery

The guest needs a realistic programme, clear meeting times, prepared staff, understandable commentary, reliable tickets, appropriate pacing, and support when plans change.

Backstage controls include itinerary feasibility, supplier confirmation, guide briefing, attraction rules, capacity, timing, communication, and service recovery.

Problem and recovery

The guest needs acknowledgment, truthful information, a realistic next step, continuity of care, and a sense that someone owns the problem.

Backstage controls include incident categorization, escalation, decision authority, approved response options, update timing, evidence, recovery cost, and closure.

Departure and final farewell

The guest needs accurate pickup timing, confidence about luggage and flight requirements, punctual movement, and a clear final handoff.

Departure is often more time-sensitive than arrival. The process must account for flight, terminal, travel time, group readiness, vehicle loading, and contingency.

Post-service learning

The guest may receive a thank-you, feedback request, complaint response, or lost-property update. Internally, the company closes records, analyzes performance, reviews suppliers, and converts learning into change.

Add the backstage layers

A useful tourism journey map has more than a line of emotions.

Guest layer

  • goal;
  • action;
  • touchpoint/channel;
  • question or information need;
  • physical and accessibility need;
  • emotion or confidence;
  • pain point; and
  • desired experience.

Frontstage layer

  • employee or supplier the guest sees;
  • visible action;
  • spoken or written communication;
  • timing or service standard; and
  • recovery behavior.

Backstage layer

  • process activity;
  • owner;
  • system and source of truth;
  • supplier dependency;
  • decision/authority;
  • risk/control;
  • record; and
  • measure.

Improvement layer

  • identified gap;
  • proposed change;
  • owner;
  • priority;
  • validation method; and
  • effect on the SOP, instruction, checklist, form, template, training, or KPI.

This structure connects experience insight to implementable operating change.

Use evidence to build the journey

Guest research

Use interviews, feedback, complaint narratives, survey comments, accessibility feedback, and observation. Ask about the sequence, not only satisfaction.

Questions include:

  • What were you trying to do?
  • What did you expect next?
  • Which instruction was clear or unclear?
  • When did you feel uncertain?
  • Did you know who was responsible?
  • Were your access or communication needs understood?
  • What helped restore confidence?

Operational evidence

Use timelines, manifests, call logs, message histories, incident records, supplier confirmations, and system timestamps. Protect personal information and obtain appropriate authorization.

Employee and supplier insight

Front-line people often know where guests become confused. They also understand constraints that journey workshops may overlook: airport access, hotel loading points, venue security, route conditions, system limits, staffing windows, and contract boundaries.

Direct observation

Walk the journey where possible. Try to find the meeting point using the actual message. Follow the accessible route. Observe where signage stops. Watch the hotel-departure flow. Test a contact channel after hours.

Do not assume that a documented service is findable or usable.

Translate guest pain points into process requirements

Pain point: “I did not know where to meet the representative.”

Do not solve this only by rewriting the message.

Check:

  • who owns meeting-point accuracy;
  • how terminal or location changes are monitored;
  • whether the message uses guest-friendly landmarks;
  • translation and accessibility;
  • when the message is sent;
  • whether the representative’s sign is consistent;
  • what the guest does if the team is not visible; and
  • how the company tests the instruction.

Pain point: “I repeated my needs to several people.”

Map requirement capture, consent, privacy, handoff, supplier acceptance, and field confirmation. Repetition may indicate that teams do not trust the data or cannot access it.

Pain point: “No one told us why the coach was late.”

Map detection, escalation, decision authority, communication ownership, update interval, approved message, and alternative. The issue may be missing operational information, not employee attitude.

Pain point: “Everyone completed a form, but nobody owned the problem.”

Clarify case ownership, handoff acceptance, closure, and follow-up. Documentation without accountability creates administrative service rather than recovery.

Design accessible journeys as a system

Accessibility cannot be a final checklist item. It must flow through policy, product information, booking, communication, transport, venue/hotel interfaces, staff competence, supplier confirmation, emergency planning, and feedback.

Ask at each stage:

  • Can the guest obtain and understand the information?
  • Can the guest communicate requirements through an appropriate channel?
  • Is consent and privacy handled correctly?
  • Does the next provider receive and accept the requirement?
  • Is the physical route and service suitable?
  • Is a dignified alternative available if the plan fails?
  • Are employees trained to assist without assumptions?
  • Is the outcome recorded and reviewed?

ISO 21902 applies across tourism stakeholders and the supply chain. Organizations still need to validate local accessibility obligations, infrastructure, and individual arrangements with qualified expertise.

Add emotion without becoming vague

Emotional mapping is useful when it leads to an operating question.

Guest stateOperational interpretation
Uncertain before arrivalConfirmation, timing, contact, or expectation may be unclear.
Anxious at meeting pointVisibility, location, wait information, or ownership may be weak.
Frustrated during delayDetection, update timing, explanation, or alternatives may be inadequate.
ExcludedAccess needs may not have been captured, accepted, or delivered.
Reassured during recoveryOwnership, empathy, truthful information, and next action are working.
Confident at departureTiming, readiness, instructions, and handoff are controlled.

Do not invent emotions for a decorative curve. Use guest evidence and state uncertainty where research is limited.

Convert the journey into SOP content

The journey map should change the procedure.

  1. Purpose and scope: include the intended guest outcome, not only internal completion.
  2. Definitions: clarify guest-facing terms that employees use differently.
  3. Responsibilities: assign communication and continuity of care across handoffs.
  4. Inputs: include access, language, contact, and expectation information.
  5. Procedure: place guest touchpoints and backstage actions in the same sequence.
  6. Exceptions: define what the guest is told, by whom, and when.
  7. Tools: design messages, signage, checklists, forms, and briefings around use.
  8. Records: capture facts and consent proportionately.
  9. KPIs: combine operational, guest, accessibility, and recovery measures.
  10. Training: practice communication and handoffs, not only system steps.

SOP Writing Part 4: Exception and Escalation Management expands the disruption layer.

Measure the journey without reducing it to one score

Use a balanced set of indicators:

  • booking/requirement completeness;
  • pre-arrival message delivery and error rate;
  • guest-location time;
  • pickup and arrival performance;
  • access-requirement confirmation and delivery;
  • handoff acceptance;
  • avoidable guest contacts or repeated information;
  • delay-update timeliness;
  • complaint and recovery themes;
  • first-contact or end-to-end resolution where appropriate;
  • supplier performance; and
  • qualitative guest and employee insight.

The existing Tour Guide Quality Index shows how multiple quality dimensions can be made observable without pretending one number tells the entire story.

Common mistakes

Mapping a marketing persona instead of an operating journey

The map describes interests and social media but does not connect to service delivery, decisions, or records.

Treating every guest as the same

Important variations disappear. Segment by needs relevant to the process.

Mapping only visible touchpoints

The organization cannot implement improvement because backstage owners, systems, suppliers, and controls are missing.

Adding emotion without evidence

The map becomes a colorful assumption. Combine guest and operational data.

Solving communication problems with more messages

Guests receive repeated or conflicting updates. Fix source information and ownership first.

Ignoring accessibility until the end

The company offers improvised assistance rather than a designed, dignified journey.

Creating improvement ideas with no document impact

The workshop ends with sticky notes. Assign owners and specify which process, document, tool, training, or measure changes.

Practical tool: Dual-Layer Tourism Journey-to-SOP Map

For each journey stage, complete both guest and operating fields.

Guest/experience fieldBackstage/SOP field
Guest goalProcess objective/output
Guest actionProcess activity
Touchpoint/channelRole, system, supplier
Information neededRequired input/source/verification
Access/communication needRequirement capture, acceptance, and control
Question or uncertaintyClarification owner and response standard
Emotion/confidence evidenceRisk, control, and recovery requirement
Pain pointRoot process or handoff condition
Desired experienceService standard and observable behavior
Recovery needTrigger, authority, message, alternative, and evidence
FeedbackRecord, KPI, review, and improvement action

Test the map with one real guest journey and one disruption scenario before converting it into procedure changes.

Final perspective

An SOP should help the organization deliver an intended experience, not only complete internal tasks.

Journey mapping makes the guest visible inside process design. It connects information, access, emotion, communication, trust, and recovery to the backstage roles, systems, suppliers, decisions, records, and measures that produce them.

When the journey and process are mapped together, the company can write procedures that work for operations and make sense to the person travelling through them.

Continue the series

  • Procedures, Processes and Process Maps: What Is the Difference?
  • Never Write an SOP Before Mapping the Process
  • SOP Writing Part 4: Exception and Escalation Management
  • Existing portfolio: From Airport Arrival to Final Farewell
  • Existing portfolio: The Guest Experience AI Toolkit

Sources and further reading

  • ISO 23592:2021, Service excellence — Principles and model
  • ISO/TS 24082:2021, Designing excellent service
  • ISO 21902:2021, Accessible tourism for all
  • ISO 22483:2020, Hotels — Service requirements
  • UN Tourism, Policy and Destination Management
  • UN Tourism, Abu Dhabi QUEST recognition

Editorial note: Journey examples are illustrative. Guest research, accessibility information, personal data, and observations must be collected and used under applicable consent, privacy, ethical, contractual, and legal requirements.

description: A professional SOP is not a long checklist and not a policy essay. It is a controlled operating document that connects purpose, scope, roles, procedure, exceptions, records, measures, approval, and revision.
html:
A professional SOP is not a long checklist and not a policy essay. It is a controlled operating document that connects purpose, scope, roles, procedure, exceptions, records, measures, approval, and revision.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S10
Audience
Tourism process owners, operations managers, quality teams, trainers, and SOP writers
Practical tool
Professional Tourism SOP Master Template
Running example
Airport Arrival Transfer SOP

Structure is a control decision

Two procedures can contain the same basic information and perform very differently.

One begins with six pages of background, hides responsibilities inside paragraphs, mixes normal and exceptional steps, uses inconsistent terms, and ends without records or ownership. The other lets a manager confirm the scope, an employee find the required action, a trainer explain the control, and an auditor trace the evidence.

The difference is not decoration. It is structure.

ISO 10013:2021 gives guidance for documented information that supports an effective quality management system and emphasizes tailoring to organizational need. It does not publish one compulsory SOP template. The structure in this article is a practical tourism model designed for operations that combine guest service, logistics, suppliers, systems, time thresholds, and live exceptions.

The template should be adapted. A simple back-office task may need a short procedure. A high-risk, multi-party airport or MICE process may need a fuller SOP with referenced instructions and tools. What should remain consistent is the logic: the document must explain why it exists, where it applies, who owns decisions, how work is performed, what happens when conditions change, and what evidence shows the result.

The complete SOP architecture

A professional tourism SOP can use the following sections:

  1. Document control information
  2. Title
  3. Purpose
  4. Scope
  5. Intended outcomes and service standards
  6. Definitions and abbreviations
  7. References and related documents
  8. Roles, responsibilities, and authority
  9. Preconditions, inputs, and required resources
  10. Procedure
  11. Exceptions, escalation, and contingency
  12. Communication requirements
  13. Records and retention
  14. Performance measures and monitoring
  15. Training and competence
  16. Approval, effective date, review, and revision history

Not every SOP needs sixteen visible headings. Related sections may be combined when clarity improves. Do not remove a control merely to make the document shorter.

1. Document control information

The reader must be able to identify the document and confirm that it is current.

Include, as appropriate:

  • document identifier;
  • title;
  • process/department;
  • owner;
  • approver(s);
  • version;
  • status;
  • effective date;
  • next review date or review trigger;
  • information classification;
  • source-of-truth location; and
  • superseded document.

Example:

FieldExample
Document IDOPS-APT-SOP-001
TitleAirport Arrival Transfer SOP
OwnerAirport Operations Manager
ApproverHead of Operations
Version1.0
Effective date[Approved date]
StatusControlled — Effective
ReviewAnnual or on material process/requirement change

Do not use “Final,” “Final 2,” or a date in the filename as the only version-control method. Document Control & Version Management provides the full lifecycle.

2. Title

Use a title that describes the controlled process, not the department or a vague concept.

Strong: Airport Arrival Transfer SOP

Weak: Airport Operations

Weak: Guest Service Procedure

The title should be unique within the register and consistent with the process catalogue.

3. Purpose

The purpose states why the SOP exists and the result it supports.

Example:

This SOP defines the controlled method for preparing, operating, monitoring, and closing confirmed airport arrival transfers so that guests are met at the approved location and delivered to the correct destination with appropriate service, safety, accessibility, communication, evidence, and exception management.

Avoid generic language such as “to ensure efficiency and quality.” State the process and the result.

4. Scope

Scope defines where the SOP starts and ends, which services, locations, teams, and suppliers it covers, and any exclusions.

Example:

Applies to confirmed individual and group arrival transfers operated or coordinated by the company from designated airports to approved hotels or venues. Begins when the approved booking is released to Operations and ends when the guest delivery, required status updates, records, and closure activities are complete. Charter operations, airside services, medical transport, and authority-controlled emergency response are outside scope unless separately approved.

Scope prevents the SOP from being stretched into situations it was not designed to control.

5. Intended outcomes and service standards

Define what successful execution looks like.

Possible outcomes:

  • confirmed information available by the required cutoff;
  • suitable team and vehicle assigned and ready;
  • flight and terminal monitored;
  • guest met or exception managed according to the approved thresholds;
  • accessible and other confirmed service needs delivered;
  • guest and client communication accurate and timely;
  • service completed and evidenced; and
  • exceptions reviewed for learning.

If numeric service standards exist, reference the controlled standard or contract rather than duplicating values likely to vary by client or service category.

6. Definitions and abbreviations

Define terms that could affect action or interpretation.

Examples:

  • Arrival wave: one or more flights or guest groups managed as a coordinated operating window.
  • Meeting point: the current location approved for the relevant terminal/service.
  • Potential no-show: a confirmed guest not located after the defined initial checks; not yet a final no-show decision.
  • Service owner: the role accountable for end-to-end control of the transfer.
  • Material change: a change that affects timing, location, resource, guest requirement, cost, safety, accessibility, or contractual delivery.

Do not fill the section with common words. Define terms that control decisions.

7. References and related documents

Show the document’s place in the operating system.

Possible references:

  • Guest Service and Safety Policy;
  • Airport Transfer Process Map;
  • Operational Authority Matrix;
  • Verify Flight Status Work Instruction;
  • Airport Readiness Checklist;
  • Guest No-Show Form;
  • Delay and Missing-Guest Message Templates;
  • Incident and Escalation Procedure;
  • Business Continuity Plan; and
  • applicable client, airport, authority, supplier, or contractual requirements.

Reference controlled sources. Do not paste the entire content of every related document into the SOP.

8. Roles, responsibilities, and authority

Describe roles before steps so readers understand ownership.

Process owner

  • owns end-to-end performance, review, risk, and improvement;
  • approves operational design changes within authority; and
  • coordinates cross-functional issues.

Reservations or handover role

  • validates booking information;
  • releases the service through the approved channel; and
  • manages late changes according to the rule.

Operations/dispatcher

  • validates operational readiness;
  • assigns resources;
  • monitors flight and vehicle status;
  • coordinates exceptions; and
  • maintains the operating picture and records.

Airport representative

  • attends the approved location;
  • maintains visibility and guest care;
  • verifies guest against the current manifest;
  • coordinates loading and handoff; and
  • reports status and exceptions.

Driver/transport supplier

  • confirms assigned service and readiness;
  • operates the vehicle according to approved requirements;
  • coordinates with the representative/dispatcher; and
  • reports completion or exception.

Duty manager

  • decides escalated issues within authority;
  • approves defined cost or service changes; and
  • activates higher-level continuity or emergency arrangements when thresholds are met.

Responsibilities should align with the process map and contracts. Avoid listing names; use roles.

9. Preconditions, inputs, and required resources

Define what must be available before execution.

Possible inputs:

  • approved booking and reference;
  • current passenger/guest manifest;
  • flight, terminal, date, and origin;
  • hotel/venue destination;
  • approved pickup/meeting instructions;
  • contact and communication permissions;
  • accessibility and special service requirements;
  • assigned representative, driver, and suitable vehicle;
  • supplier confirmation;
  • signage/identification;
  • approved systems and fallback information; and
  • client-specific conditions.

State what happens when an input is missing. “Ensure information is complete” is not enough. Define who returns, corrects, accepts, or escalates the service and by when.

10. Procedure

The procedure section follows the validated process sequence. Use numbered stages and conditional instructions.

Stage 1 — Receive and validate the service

  1. Reservations releases the approved booking through the designated source.
  2. Operations verifies mandatory information against the process requirements.
  3. Missing, conflicting, or changed information is returned or escalated through the approved path.
  4. Operations records acceptance and current status.

Stage 2 — Assign and confirm resources

  1. Operations assigns a representative, driver, and vehicle appropriate to the service and confirmed guest requirements.
  2. Suppliers receive the current service details through the approved channel.
  3. Acceptance must confirm the critical fields, not only acknowledge receipt.
  4. Unconfirmed or unsuitable resources follow the escalation and replacement path.

Stage 3 — Complete readiness checks

  1. The representative verifies reporting time, terminal, meeting point, manifest, signage, contact route, and special requirements.
  2. Transport verifies vehicle and driver readiness according to the applicable control.
  3. Operations reviews unresolved exceptions before the cutoff.

Stage 4 — Monitor arrival

  1. Operations begins flight monitoring at the approved time.
  2. Material changes are recorded and communicated to affected roles.
  3. Early arrival, delay, terminal change, cancellation, or missed connection follows the defined exception path.

Stage 5 — Meet and identify the guest

  1. The representative reports at the approved location and maintains the required visibility.
  2. The representative verifies the guest against the current manifest using proportionate identification controls.
  3. The representative provides the approved welcome and next-step information.
  4. Unlisted, missing, or incorrectly matched guests are not improvised into the service; the exception route applies.

Stage 6 — Load and release the vehicle

  1. The representative and driver coordinate luggage, guest count, confirmed support, and vehicle readiness.
  2. Departure status is communicated through the approved operating source.
  3. Vehicle release follows the waiting, missing-guest, and authority rules.

Stage 7 — Operate and complete the transfer

  1. The driver follows the approved destination and service information.
  2. Material route, guest, vehicle, or destination changes are reported.
  3. Arrival is confirmed at the agreed destination/handoff.

Stage 8 — Close the service

  1. Required completion and exception records are finalized.
  2. Operations updates the service status and identifies unresolved actions.
  3. The service is released for reconciliation only when closure criteria are satisfied.

The next masterclass article will develop sentence-level procedure writing, action verbs, sequence, time standards, and conditional logic.

11. Exceptions, escalation, and contingency

Define categories and triggers, not a generic statement.

Examples:

  • missing or conflicting booking information;
  • flight early, delayed, cancelled, or moved;
  • guest not on manifest;
  • guest not located;
  • baggage delay;
  • unsuitable or unready vehicle;
  • staff absence;
  • inaccessible route or service;
  • hotel/venue change;
  • system or communications outage;
  • medical, safety, security, or emergency condition; and
  • supplier failure.

For each material exception, define first response, owner, response time, authority, guest/client communication, evidence, fallback, and closure. SOP Writing Part 4: Exception and Escalation Management provides the full model.

An SOP should also state when a situation leaves its scope and activates a business-continuity, crisis, emergency, security, medical, or authority-controlled plan.

12. Communication requirements

Define communication that is operationally necessary:

  • who communicates;
  • audience;
  • trigger;
  • channel;
  • minimum facts;
  • approval where required;
  • update interval;
  • language/accessibility consideration;
  • privacy restriction; and
  • record.

Use templates as controlled starting points, not messages sent without verification.

13. Records and retention

List the records created and the system of record.

Examples:

  • accepted booking/handover;
  • resource confirmations;
  • readiness checklist;
  • manifest and movement status;
  • flight-change record;
  • guest-search/no-show form;
  • authorization;
  • guest/client communication;
  • incident record; and
  • service completion.

Define owner, access, retention, and disposal through the organization’s record-control requirements. Do not collect personal data without a purpose.

14. Performance measures and monitoring

Possible measures:

  • booking completeness at handover;
  • resource confirmation by cutoff;
  • readiness exceptions;
  • representative/vehicle readiness;
  • guest-location or no-show exceptions;
  • on-time completion under the approved definition;
  • accessibility requirement delivery;
  • record completeness;
  • complaints/recovery; and
  • repeated exceptions by cause.

Define source, formula, frequency, owner, threshold, and action. Avoid metrics that encourage unsafe speed or conceal complexity.

15. Training and competence

State which roles require training, practice, assessment, and refresher triggers.

The competence method may include:

  • briefing on purpose and controls;
  • guided review of role-specific sections;
  • system/task demonstration;
  • scenario practice;
  • observed performance;
  • assessment and authorization; and
  • refresher after change, incident, poor performance, or extended absence.

Distribution is not training, and training attendance is not competence.

16. Approval, effective date, review, and revision history

The revision history should explain material changes.

VersionDateChangeOwner/approver
0.1DraftInitial process-owner draft[Role]
0.2ReviewField pilot and exception changes[Role]
1.0EffectiveFirst approved release[Role]

Define review triggers such as process redesign, system change, client/contract change, legal or authority requirement, supplier change, incident, audit finding, or performance deterioration. An annual review should not prevent immediate change when risk is material.

Writing rules for usable SOPs

Use one accountable action per sentence

Weak: “The manifest should be checked and if there are any problems they should be dealt with.”

Stronger: “Operations verifies the mandatory manifest fields before accepting the service. Missing or conflicting information is returned to Reservations through the late-change workflow.”

Name the role

Avoid “someone,” “the team,” or passive language when accountability matters.

Use conditional logic

Write: “If the flight terminal changes after the representative reports, Dispatch confirms the new meeting arrangement and records the update before instructing movement.”

Do not hide decisions in notes.

Use measurable terms

“Promptly,” “early,” “regularly,” and “where possible” require defined meaning or judgement guidance. Reference approved thresholds where values vary.

Keep stable and volatile content separate

Stable process control belongs in the SOP. Frequently changing system screens, contact lists, rates, or location details may belong in controlled instructions, registers, or tools.

Write for point-of-work use

Use clear headings, numbered stages, short paragraphs, tables only for true comparison, and direct references to tools. Test on the device and environment employees use.

Review the draft through four lenses

Operational lens

Can the user perform the normal process? Are inputs, steps, handoffs, and closure clear?

Risk lens

Are material risks, decision points, exceptions, authority, and fallback addressed? Use the findings from How to Conduct an Operational Risk Assessment Before Writing an SOP.

Guest lens

Does the SOP support clear, accessible, respectful, and continuous service? Use the journey map.

Assurance lens

Can the organization verify current version, competence, implementation, records, measures, and improvement?

Common structure failures

Background overwhelms action

Move long rationale to training or guidance. Keep necessary context, but let users find the procedure.

Scope is missing

Employees apply the SOP to a service, location, or emergency it was not designed for.

Responsibilities repeat the job description

List process responsibilities and decision authority, not generic duties.

Exceptions appear as “notes”

Critical conditions are easy to miss. Give them a visible section and link to the exact procedure stage.

Records are undefined

The SOP requires “documentation” without naming the record, field, owner, or system.

The approval page is stronger than implementation

The document has signatures but no pilot, training, access, or usage review.

Practical tool: Professional Tourism SOP Master Template

Use this outline as the controlled drafting shell:

  1. Document control: ID, owner, approver, version, effective/review dates, status, source.
  2. Title: unique process-oriented name.
  3. Purpose: why the SOP exists and intended result.
  4. Scope: trigger, end point, services, locations, roles, exclusions.
  5. Outcomes/standards: successful result and referenced requirements.
  6. Definitions: terms that change action.
  7. References: governing policies, maps, instructions, tools, external requirements.
  8. Roles/authority: process accountability and decision limits.
  9. Preconditions/inputs: mandatory information, resources, systems, approvals.
  10. Procedure: numbered stages, actions, handoffs, decisions, and closure.
  11. Exceptions/escalation: triggers, responses, authority, communication, fallback.
  12. Communication: audience, channel, facts, timing, templates, privacy.
  13. Records: evidence, owner, system, access, retention.
  14. Measures: definitions, source, frequency, threshold, action.
  15. Training/competence: roles, method, assessment, refresher.
  16. Approval/revision: sign-off, effective date, history, change reason.

Final perspective

The best SOP structure makes the operating logic visible. It tells the reader what result matters, where the process begins and ends, who decides, what must be ready, how work flows, what changes the path, what the guest is told, what evidence is created, and how management knows the procedure still works.

A template cannot replace process discovery or professional judgement. It can prevent important control questions from disappearing.

Structure is therefore not the final formatting stage. It is part of operational design.

Continue the series

  • Policy vs SOP vs Work Instruction vs Checklist vs Form vs Template
  • SOP Writing Part 4: Exception and Escalation Management
  • Document Control & Version Management

  • Existing portfolio: The Assignment Engine

Sources and further reading

  • ISO 10013:2021, Guidance for documented information
  • ISO, The process approach in ISO 9001:2015
  • ISO 9001 explained
  • ISO 10007:2017, Guidelines for configuration management
  • ISO 31000:2018, Risk management — Guidelines
  • ISO 21902:2021, Accessible tourism for all
  • ISO 22483:2020, Hotels — Service requirements

Editorial note: The template is a recommended structure, not an ISO-prescribed format. Organizations must adapt it to applicable law, regulation, contracts, safety, accessibility, privacy, technology, competence, and service risk.

description: Turn policy intent and mapped work into instructions that identify the actor, action, sequence, decision, time standard, evidence, and exception path.
html:
Turn policy intent and mapped work into instructions that identify the actor, action, sequence, decision, time standard, evidence, and exception path.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S11
Audience
Tourism SOP authors, operations managers, quality reviewers, and process owners
Practical tool
Seven-part instruction test and annotated airport-transfer procedure
Running example
Writing the live-day section of an airport-transfer SOP

The operating problem

A professional procedure does not sound formal for its own sake. It makes the required action observable, places it in sequence, assigns it to a role, defines necessary conditions, and connects the action to evidence or escalation. Tourism work makes this discipline unusually important. A single service may join Sales, Reservations, Operations, a hotel, an airport team, a transport partner, a guide, a client, and the guest. Information changes while the service is live, and the person who notices a problem may not hold the authority to change cost, timing, supplier, or customer promise. The document therefore has to work as an operating interface, not simply as well-written office content. The starting point is the broader system described in the operating-system overview. That system separates governance, execution, evidence, measurement, and improvement. The present article focuses on one controlled component, while the document-type comparison explains why an SOP, work instruction, checklist, form, template, and record should not be asked to perform the same job. This is a practical management model, not a universal template imposed by ISO or a substitute for applicable law, contract terms, safety requirements, privacy advice, or emergency arrangements. An organization should tailor the depth, approval, terminology, and retained evidence to its services, risk, size, jurisdiction, technology, and competence. Approval should therefore be evidence-led. Reviewers should see the mapped work, representative records, relevant risk and guest requirements, user-test observations, and unresolved issues—not only the polished draft. That evidence makes the approval decision explainable and gives the owner a baseline for measuring whether the released control improves real performance.

The distinctions that prevent document failure

Purpose explains why the SOP exists; procedure explains what authorized roles do. Repeating policy language inside every step makes the document longer without making execution clearer. A procedure governs a repeatable flow. A work instruction may explain a particular system screen, device, or technical task. A checklist helps a user execute or confirm critical items without rereading the complete procedure. Mandatory language should be deliberate. ‘Shall’ or ‘must’ can signal a requirement where the organization has chosen that convention; ‘should’ normally signals a recommendation. The document-control standard should define the house style. Precision is not the same as rigidity. A good instruction can define the result, threshold, authority, and evidence while leaving trained staff discretion over guest-facing delivery within approved boundaries.

Practical tool: Seven-part instruction test and annotated airport-transfer procedure

The following canvas is designed for a working session, not decorative inclusion in a manual. Complete it using a real service and current records. Every answer should be specific enough for another role to validate.

ElementControl questionTourism example
ActorWho performs or owns the step?Airport Coordinator
ActionWhat observable verb describes the work?Confirm, compare, record, notify, authorize
ObjectWhat information, guest, asset, or record is affected?Flight status and assigned arrival resources
ConditionWhen or under what trigger does the step apply?At the defined monitoring interval or status change
StandardWhat time, quality, or acceptance rule applies?Within the service-category reporting threshold
EvidenceWhat proves completion?Timestamped update in the movement log

The table is intentionally compact. Supporting detail should live in the appropriate controlled document or system rather than expanding one tool until it becomes impossible to use. During review, mark assumptions, unresolved authority, weak inputs, and missing evidence separately; do not convert them into confident statements merely to finish the template.

A professional design workflow

1. Write from the approved map

Convert each controlled activity and decision into a draft step. Keep the same boundary, owner, and handoff language so the SOP does not invent a second version of the process.

2. Choose an observable action verb

Replace vague phrases such as ‘handle the guest’, ‘make sure’, or ‘as appropriate’ with actions a trained reviewer can recognize: verify, reconcile, escort, record, obtain approval, or escalate.

3. Name the responsible role

Use a position or operational role, not a person's name. Where a system performs an automated action, identify who monitors the outcome and who intervenes when automation fails.

4. Put normal steps in chronological order

Begin at the operational trigger and continue through closure. Separate preparation, execution, handoff, and close-out so staff can locate the stage that matches the live situation.

5. Write decisions as conditions

State the condition, the authorized response, and the next path. For example: if estimated arrival changes beyond the approved threshold, Operations reviews vehicle and representative assignments and records the decision.

6. Attach time and acceptance standards carefully

Use defined thresholds that the operation can measure. ‘Arrive early’ is not controllable; a reporting time tied to service category, access condition, or briefing instruction can be monitored.

7. Connect evidence and exceptions

Do not bolt records and escalation onto the end. At the relevant step, specify what is recorded and direct non-standard conditions to the approved exception section or escalation matrix. After completing the workflow, test the connected design during writing the live-day section of an airport-transfer sop. Ask users to work from the draft and approved tools without whispered instructions. Any dependency on a particular manager's memory should be recorded, owned, and resolved through the correct control—document, system, authority, contract, resource, or competence—before release.

Running example: Writing the live-day section of an airport-transfer SOP

Weak draft

‘The driver should arrive early and check everything’ hides the reporting time, location, assigned checks, evidence, and response to a problem.

Controlled rewrite

‘The assigned driver reports to the designated pickup location by the reporting time shown in the approved service brief and confirms readiness in the dispatch channel.’

Conditional addition

‘If access is blocked or the location differs from the service brief, the driver stops in a safe permitted area, informs Dispatch, and waits for an authorized alternative location.’

Evidence addition

Dispatch records the readiness time and any location change against the service reference, avoiding a disconnected free-text message that cannot be traced later.

Field validation

A driver, dispatcher, airport coordinator, and supervisor walk through the instruction using a real service. Their questions reveal where technical detail belongs in a work instruction or checklist.

The scenario should be validated against the service's current risk assessment and guest journey, not treated as a perfect script. Compare it with the methods in operational risk assessment before SOP writing and customer journey mapping for SOP design. Those articles help the team check whether an internally neat design also addresses operational uncertainty and the guest's visible experience.

Common failure modes—and the design response

  • Writing passive instructions with no actor. Use a recent case to show the operational consequence and identify the earliest control that could have prevented or detected it.
  • Using ‘timely’, ‘properly’, or ‘as necessary’ without a defined test. Trace the issue across roles and handoffs; the visible error may originate in an earlier input, authority decision, or system rule.
  • Mixing policy, training notes, and live steps in one paragraph. Decide whether the remedy belongs in this document, a supporting tool, the system, the contract, resource planning, or competence development.
  • Burying decisions inside long prose. Test the proposed correction in a normal case and an exception so that solving one failure does not create another downstream.
  • Creating time standards that systems do not capture. Assign an owner and evidence for the correction, then set a date to confirm that the failure has not simply moved into an unofficial workaround.
  • Ignoring the close-out and handoff steps. Where risk remains, record and escalate it explicitly rather than adding vague cautionary prose that no user can apply under pressure.

Implementation and control

  1. Adopt one procedure-writing convention. Confirm the mandate, affected processes, and release decision so ownership does not disappear after the workshop.
  2. Use a step identifier that survives revisions. Schedule the work around live operations and include every shift, location, or partner needed to validate the design.
  3. Review the draft against the process map and risk register. Keep an issue log with decision owner and due date; unresolved assumptions should never be disguised as approved instructions.
  4. Simulate normal and exception scenarios. Define the evidence of readiness—approved content, system access, supporting tools, briefed partners, competent users, and supervisor cover.
  5. Approve related work instructions, checklists, forms, and templates as a controlled pack. Set an early-use review and a routine review trigger, then route defects, competence gaps, and resource problems to different actions.

Implementation should be staged. Begin with a representative service, observe use, and correct design defects before large-scale release. Control the approved version through document control and version management, and use training, competency, and SOP adoption to distinguish a distribution list from genuine competence and adoption.

Measures that show whether the control works

A useful measure should help the owner decide, not simply make a dashboard look complete. Establish a definition, data source, owner, review frequency, context, and action threshold for each selected measure.

Candidate measureWhat the owner should learn
Steps passed during field simulationWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Clarification calls during live useWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Missed handoffs per 100 servicesWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Evidence completeness at close-outWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Exceptions caused by ambiguous instructionsWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome

Do not read one indicator in isolation. A perfect completion rate alongside rising clarification calls may indicate retrospective box-ticking. A temporary increase in reported exceptions can be healthy after training if staff have begun recording issues that were previously hidden. Pair compliance, outcome, user-friction, guest, and improvement signals.

Field review before approval

Boundary

Does the document begin and end at points the team can identify, or does it absorb adjacent processes until no owner can validate it? State the trigger, completion condition, excluded work, and connected processes. Then follow one real job reference from start to finish and note every point where the draft crosses its own boundary.

Roles and authority

Can every action and decision be traced to a current role, deputy, authority level, and escalation path across shifts and partners? Compare the draft with rosters, job descriptions, delegation limits, and partner contacts. Ask the night or weekend shift who actually decides when the named manager is unavailable.

Time and sequence

Are triggers, deadlines, intervals, pause points, and handoffs measurable in the systems and working conditions actually used? Use timestamps from a normal case and a disrupted case. Replace vague timing with an observable event or controlled threshold, and confirm that the relevant system or record can capture it.

Information quality

Are required inputs current, traceable, appropriately protected, and presented in a form that the receiving role can use without reinterpretation? Trace each critical value to its source, owner, format, and latest valid version. Resolve duplicate fields and define what the receiver does when two approved-looking sources disagree.

Exceptions

Has the team tested delay, absence, conflicting information, technology failure, supplier failure, accessibility needs, and a changing guest situation? Run at least one scenario that exceeds front-line authority. Observe whether staff can recognize the trigger, stabilize the service, escalate with the right facts, communicate, and return the case to controlled closure.

Evidence

Does the record capture timely facts, source, action, authority, and outcome without unnecessary personal data, speculation, or retrospective reconstruction? Reconstruct a recent event using only retained records. Missing links reveal where the design needs a prompt, automatic timestamp, approval trace, attachment rule, or clearer close-out responsibility.

Guest experience

Does the control protect the guest's clarity, dignity, accessibility, time, and communication needs as well as the company's internal workflow? Walk through what the guest sees, hears, waits for, and must do. Check language, channel, physical access, assistance, uncertainty, and recovery rather than assuming internal compliance equals a good experience.

Usability

Can representative users perform the work on the actual device or paper format, under interruption and time pressure, without unofficial notes? Watch rather than coach. Record where users pause, scroll, search, abbreviate, take screenshots, or switch to personal tools; those behaviors are design evidence, not merely user resistance.

Partner interface

Do external providers understand the same requirement, status, contact, evidence, and change rules, including the right to raise a concern early? Ask the partner to explain the handoff in their own words and demonstrate the communication route. Resolve differences before release, especially around substitutions, delay, cost, guest contact, and retained evidence.

Learning and review

Will operational data, user feedback, complaints, audits, and change triggers lead to a controlled revision rather than a parallel workaround? Name who reviews which signals, how often, and what action threshold applies. Connect urgent correction, routine revision, refresher training, supplier action, and formal improvement to distinct governance routes.

How this article connects to the series

The most useful next readings are the professional SOP structure, roles, authority, and RACI, work-instruction design. These links are conceptual rather than promotional: each one supplies a prerequisite, supporting control, or next implementation step. A reader should be able to follow the series from system design to live use and improvement without encountering a forced link in every paragraph. The portfolio already shows the operating context in The Assignment Engine, Before the Delegate Reaches the Hotel, The Abu Dhabi MICE Movement Control Room. Those pieces provide concrete examples of journeys, dashboards, assignments, quality tools, commercial controls, partner handoffs, or service recovery. This article extends them by explaining the management method behind reliable execution.

Manager's release checklist

  • The purpose, boundary, users, owner, and approval authority are explicit.
  • The content matches the approved process map, risk assessment, customer journey, and current systems.
  • Roles, deputies, thresholds, evidence, privacy, accessibility, supplier interfaces, and exceptions have been tested.
  • Supporting SOPs, work instructions, checklists, forms, templates, records, and training do not contradict one another.
  • Representative users have completed a normal and exception scenario in the actual work environment.
  • The release, access, version, change, retention, review, and withdrawal controls are ready before go-live.

Sources and further reading

  • ISO 10013:2021 — guidance for documented information
  • ISO/TC 176 guidance on ISO 9001 documented information
  • NASA procedural requirements for specific, owned requirements statements
  • FAA Human Factors Design Standard — user documentation

Editorial note: This article provides operational and quality-management guidance for a professional portfolio. It does not provide legal, regulatory, privacy, safety, emergency, employment, or contractual advice. Apply qualified local review wherever those obligations affect the service.

description: Define who performs the work, who owns the outcome, who contributes before a decision, who receives information, and where operational authority stops.
