Define who performs the work, who owns the outcome, who contributes before a decision, who receives information, and where operational authority stops.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S12
Audience
Tourism process owners, duty managers, quality teams, project leads, and cross-functional SOP authors
Practical tool
Tourism RACI and decision-authority matrix
Running example
A delayed coach movement involving Operations, the hotel, transport supplier, guide, client, and guest communications

The operating problem

RACI helps expose responsibility gaps, but a professional SOP must go further. It must identify decision rights, financial limits, communication authority, deputies, shift handoffs, and escalation conditions. Tourism work makes this discipline unusually important. A single service may join Sales, Reservations, Operations, a hotel, an airport team, a transport partner, a guide, a client, and the guest. Information changes while the service is live, and the person who notices a problem may not hold the authority to change cost, timing, supplier, or customer promise. The document therefore has to work as an operating interface, not simply as well-written office content. The starting point is the broader system described in the operating-system overview. That system separates governance, execution, evidence, measurement, and improvement. The present article focuses on one controlled component, while the document-type comparison explains why an SOP, work instruction, checklist, form, template, and record should not be asked to perform the same job. This is a practical management model, not a universal template imposed by ISO or a substitute for applicable law, contract terms, safety requirements, privacy advice, or emergency arrangements. An organization should tailor the depth, approval, terminology, and retained evidence to its services, risk, size, jurisdiction, technology, and competence. Approval should therefore be evidence-led. Reviewers should see the mapped work, representative records, relevant risk and guest requirements, user-test observations, and unresolved issues—not only the polished draft. That evidence makes the approval decision explainable and gives the owner a baseline for measuring whether the released control improves real performance.

The distinctions that prevent document failure

Responsible is the role doing or coordinating the work. Accountable is the role answerable for the result and approval. Consulted roles provide input before action; informed roles receive relevant information after or during the event. A RACI row should describe an outcome or meaningful activity. If rows are every mouse click, the matrix becomes unreadable; if a row says only ‘operations’, it is too broad to expose ownership. Accountability does not automatically grant unlimited authority. A duty manager may own service recovery while needing commercial approval above a defined additional-cost threshold. Communication responsibility is separate from decision authority. One manager may approve the alternative coach while an assigned guest-facing role communicates the verified plan using the approved message.

Practical tool: Tourism RACI and decision-authority matrix

The following canvas is designed for a working session, not decorative inclusion in a manual. Complete it using a real service and current records. Every answer should be specific enough for another role to validate.

ElementControl questionTourism example
R — ResponsibleWho performs or coordinates the work?Movement Controller
A — AccountableWho owns the result and final decision?Duty Operations Manager
C — ConsultedWhose input is required before action?Hotel, transport partner, client account lead
I — InformedWho needs the verified outcome?Guide, travel desk, Finance, next shift
AuthorityWhat may the accountable role authorize?Alternative resource within approved limit
EscalationWhat exceeds that authority?Safety event, cancellation, public statement, higher cost

The table is intentionally compact. Supporting detail should live in the appropriate controlled document or system rather than expanding one tool until it becomes impossible to use. During review, mark assumptions, unresolved authority, weak inputs, and missing evidence separately; do not convert them into confident statements merely to finish the template.

A professional design workflow

1. List operational outcomes

Begin with the process map: validate booking, approve assignment, confirm readiness, control live movement, authorize recovery, communicate with the guest, close the record.

2. Assign responsibility to roles

Use role titles that exist on the roster and organization chart. Avoid writing ‘team’ where one person must act, and define the handoff when responsibility passes between shifts or locations.

3. Set one accountable owner where practical

Multiple A entries often mean the decision has not been resolved. When governance genuinely requires joint approval, state the rule and response time rather than hiding it inside a matrix.

4. Define consultation with a deadline

Consulted does not mean every stakeholder comments on everything. Identify the question they answer, channel, and latest useful response time so consultation does not paralyze live operations.

5. Add authority limits

For cost, cancellation, complimentary service, supplier replacement, data release, and public communication, document what each operational level may authorize and what must be escalated.

6. Test deputies and absence

Night shifts, weekends, overlapping groups, and remote partners expose governance that works only when named managers are present. Define acting authority and record how the transfer is acknowledged. After completing the workflow, test the connected design during a delayed coach movement involving operations, the hotel, transport supplier, guide, client, and guest communications. Ask users to work from the draft and approved tools without whispered instructions. Any dependency on a particular manager's memory should be recorded, owned, and resolved through the correct control—document, system, authority, contract, resource, or competence—before release.

Running example: A delayed coach movement involving Operations, the hotel, transport supplier, guide, client, and guest communications

Trigger

A coach reports a mechanical warning forty minutes before a hotel departure. The supplier is Responsible for technical assessment; the Movement Controller is Responsible for coordination.

Decision

The Duty Operations Manager is Accountable for the service response and can approve a replacement within the agreed commercial limit. Higher cost or cancellation goes to the Operations Director.

Consultation

The hotel desk provides loading status and holding options; the supplier provides replacement ETA; the client account lead is consulted if the change affects the programme.

Communication

The Guide receives the approved operational message and updates guests. No one speculates about technical causes or promises compensation without authority.

Closure

The controller records the decision, approval, communications, revised departure, and supplier follow-up. Finance and the next shift are informed through the controlled record.

The scenario should be validated against the service's current risk assessment and guest journey, not treated as a perfect script. Compare it with the methods in operational risk assessment before SOP writing and customer journey mapping for SOP design. Those articles help the team check whether an internally neat design also addresses operational uncertainty and the guest's visible experience.

Common failure modes—and the design response

  • Assigning raci letters to departments that do not recognize the task. Use a recent case to show the operational consequence and identify the earliest control that could have prevented or detected it.
  • Placing more than one unexplained accountable owner on every row. Trace the issue across roles and handoffs; the visible error may originate in an earlier input, authority decision, or system rule.
  • Confusing ‘consulted’ with permission to delay a live decision. Decide whether the remedy belongs in this document, a supporting tool, the system, the contract, resource planning, or competence development.
  • Omitting deputies and shift transfer. Test the proposed correction in a normal case and an exception so that solving one failure does not create another downstream.
  • Failing to separate operational, commercial, and communication authority. Assign an owner and evidence for the correction, then set a date to confirm that the failure has not simply moved into an unofficial workaround.
  • Publishing a matrix inconsistent with job descriptions or contracts. Where risk remains, record and escalate it explicitly rather than adding vague cautionary prose that no user can apply under pressure.

Implementation and control

  1. Facilitate the first matrix with all affected roles. Confirm the mandate, affected processes, and release decision so ownership does not disappear after the workshop.
  2. Pair raci with an authority-and-escalation schedule. Schedule the work around live operations and include every shift, location, or partner needed to validate the design.
  3. Validate role names against rosters and partner agreements. Keep an issue log with decision owner and due date; unresolved assumptions should never be disguised as approved instructions.
  4. Include raci scenarios in training. Define the evidence of readiness—approved content, system access, supporting tools, briefed partners, competent users, and supervisor cover.
  5. Control matrix changes with the sop revision. Set an early-use review and a routine review trigger, then route defects, competence gaps, and resource problems to different actions.

Implementation should be staged. Begin with a representative service, observe use, and correct design defects before large-scale release. Control the approved version through document control and version management, and use training, competency, and SOP adoption to distinguish a distribution list from genuine competence and adoption.

Measures that show whether the control works

A useful measure should help the owner decide, not simply make a dashboard look complete. Establish a definition, data source, owner, review frequency, context, and action threshold for each selected measure.

Candidate measureWhat the owner should learn
Decisions made within authority and target timeWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Escalations returned for missing informationWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Duplicate or conflicting instructionsWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Unowned actions found in auditsWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Handoffs acknowledged by the receiving roleWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome

Do not read one indicator in isolation. A perfect completion rate alongside rising clarification calls may indicate retrospective box-ticking. A temporary increase in reported exceptions can be healthy after training if staff have begun recording issues that were previously hidden. Pair compliance, outcome, user-friction, guest, and improvement signals.

Field review before approval

Boundary

Does the document begin and end at points the team can identify, or does it absorb adjacent processes until no owner can validate it? State the trigger, completion condition, excluded work, and connected processes. Then follow one real job reference from start to finish and note every point where the draft crosses its own boundary.

Roles and authority

Can every action and decision be traced to a current role, deputy, authority level, and escalation path across shifts and partners? Compare the draft with rosters, job descriptions, delegation limits, and partner contacts. Ask the night or weekend shift who actually decides when the named manager is unavailable.

Time and sequence

Are triggers, deadlines, intervals, pause points, and handoffs measurable in the systems and working conditions actually used? Use timestamps from a normal case and a disrupted case. Replace vague timing with an observable event or controlled threshold, and confirm that the relevant system or record can capture it.

Information quality

Are required inputs current, traceable, appropriately protected, and presented in a form that the receiving role can use without reinterpretation? Trace each critical value to its source, owner, format, and latest valid version. Resolve duplicate fields and define what the receiver does when two approved-looking sources disagree.

Exceptions

Has the team tested delay, absence, conflicting information, technology failure, supplier failure, accessibility needs, and a changing guest situation? Run at least one scenario that exceeds front-line authority. Observe whether staff can recognize the trigger, stabilize the service, escalate with the right facts, communicate, and return the case to controlled closure.

Evidence

Does the record capture timely facts, source, action, authority, and outcome without unnecessary personal data, speculation, or retrospective reconstruction? Reconstruct a recent event using only retained records. Missing links reveal where the design needs a prompt, automatic timestamp, approval trace, attachment rule, or clearer close-out responsibility.

Guest experience

Does the control protect the guest's clarity, dignity, accessibility, time, and communication needs as well as the company's internal workflow? Walk through what the guest sees, hears, waits for, and must do. Check language, channel, physical access, assistance, uncertainty, and recovery rather than assuming internal compliance equals a good experience.

Usability

Can representative users perform the work on the actual device or paper format, under interruption and time pressure, without unofficial notes? Watch rather than coach. Record where users pause, scroll, search, abbreviate, take screenshots, or switch to personal tools; those behaviors are design evidence, not merely user resistance.

Partner interface

Do external providers understand the same requirement, status, contact, evidence, and change rules, including the right to raise a concern early? Ask the partner to explain the handoff in their own words and demonstrate the communication route. Resolve differences before release, especially around substitutions, delay, cost, guest contact, and retained evidence.

Learning and review

Will operational data, user feedback, complaints, audits, and change triggers lead to a controlled revision rather than a parallel workaround? Name who reviews which signals, how often, and what action threshold applies. Connect urgent correction, routine revision, refresher training, supplier action, and formal improvement to distinct governance routes.

How this article connects to the series

The most useful next readings are the professional SOP structure, exception and escalation management, training, competency, and SOP adoption. These links are conceptual rather than promotional: each one supplies a prerequisite, supporting control, or next implementation step. A reader should be able to follow the series from system design to live use and improvement without encountering a forced link in every paragraph. The portfolio already shows the operating context in Tourism Operations Roles, The Assignment Engine, The Abu Dhabi MICE Movement Control Room. Those pieces provide concrete examples of journeys, dashboards, assignments, quality tools, commercial controls, partner handoffs, or service recovery. This article extends them by explaining the management method behind reliable execution.

Manager's release checklist

  • The purpose, boundary, users, owner, and approval authority are explicit.
  • The content matches the approved process map, risk assessment, customer journey, and current systems.
  • Roles, deputies, thresholds, evidence, privacy, accessibility, supplier interfaces, and exceptions have been tested.
  • Supporting SOPs, work instructions, checklists, forms, templates, records, and training do not contradict one another.
  • Representative users have completed a normal and exception scenario in the actual work environment.
  • The release, access, version, change, retention, review, and withdrawal controls are ready before go-live.

Sources and further reading

  • Project Management Institute — Responsibility Assignment Matrix and RACI
  • ISO 10013:2021 — guidance for documented information
  • NASA procedural requirements for specific, owned requirements statements
  • ISO 31000:2018 — risk management guidelines

Editorial note: This article provides operational and quality-management guidance for a professional portfolio. It does not provide legal, regulatory, privacy, safety, emergency, employment, or contractual advice. Apply qualified local review wherever those obligations affect the service.

description: A procedure becomes operationally credible when it explains not only the normal path, but also how people recognize a deviation, stabilize the service, obtain authority, communicate, record decisions, recover, and learn.
html:
A procedure becomes operationally credible when it explains not only the normal path, but also how people recognize a deviation, stabilize the service, obtain authority, communicate, record decisions, recover, and learn.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S13
Audience
Tourism operations managers, duty managers, process owners, quality teams, event controllers, and SOP writers
Practical tool
Exception and Escalation Matrix
Running example
A MICE airport-to-hotel movement with simultaneous disruptions

The paragraph that weakens many SOPs

“In case of any issue, contact the manager.”

It is one of the most common sentences in operating documents, and one of the least useful. It does not define an issue, indicate when the normal process is no longer safe or achievable, identify which manager is on duty, set a response time, explain what the frontline team may do while waiting, or describe the information needed for a decision.

Tourism rarely runs in a perfectly controlled environment. Flights arrive early, guests change plans, baggage is delayed, roads close, suppliers substitute resources, systems stop responding, weather affects an activity, and a client requests a change during delivery. An SOP that covers only the expected sequence leaves its most important decisions to memory and improvisation.

Exception management does not mean writing a script for every imaginable problem. It means designing a controlled method for departures from the expected path. The method should help the team identify the condition, protect people and the service, distinguish operational authority from emergency authority, select an approved response, communicate accurately, keep evidence, and return to a stable state.

This is where procedure, risk, continuity, customer care, and management authority meet.

Define the levels before writing responses

Teams often use “issue,” “incident,” “emergency,” and “crisis” as if they mean the same thing. The labels themselves matter less than a shared, approved classification. One practical model is:

LevelWorking definitionTypical control need
DeviationA departure from the planned or standard condition that can still be managed within the assigned role and approved tolerancesCorrect, record where required, and continue
Operational exceptionA condition requiring a decision, resource, or coordination outside the normal step but within routine duty-management capabilityEscalate to the designated operational owner and manage against a response time
IncidentAn event with material effect or credible potential effect on people, service, information, property, cost, contract, or reputationStabilize, notify the designated incident role, preserve records, and manage formally
Major incidentAn incident whose scale, severity, duration, or dependencies exceed routine operational controlActivate cross-functional or senior management coordination and relevant plans
EmergencyA situation requiring immediate protective action and, where applicable, competent emergency services or authority responseProtect life and safety, follow local emergency requirements, then support authorized response
CrisisA situation that threatens strategic objectives, trust, or organizational viability and requires executive-level coordinationActivate crisis governance and communication arrangements

These are illustrative definitions, not universal legal categories. A company should align them with applicable law, authority guidance, contracts, insurance, venue or airport rules, and its business-continuity and emergency plans.

The distinction matters because different situations require different command structures. A delayed coach is usually an operational exception. A collision with injuries is not a “transport delay” to be solved only by dispatch. The team must know when local emergency procedures take priority and when business-continuity arrangements support, rather than replace, the competent response.

Start with the objective and tolerances

Every exception is a departure from an expected condition. The SOP therefore needs an explicit operating objective and meaningful tolerances.

For a MICE arrival movement, the objective may be to receive confirmed delegates, care for them at the arrival point, allocate them to the correct transport, and deliver them to the designated hotel within the approved programme and service conditions.

Tolerances may cover:

  • minimum confirmed vehicle capacity;
  • allowable dispatch variation;
  • maximum waiting period before the next decision;
  • information cutoff for manifest changes;
  • cost authority by role;
  • approved substitution rules;
  • service, accessibility, and safeguarding conditions;
  • client-notification thresholds; and
  • evidence required before closure.

A tolerance is not permission to conceal poor performance. It is an approved boundary within which a role can act without unnecessary escalation. If the situation moves outside that boundary, the next decision owner becomes clear.

The risk assessment should determine which tolerances and triggers are necessary. See How to Conduct an Operational Risk Assessment Before Writing an SOP.

Design the escalation architecture

An effective escalation path answers seven questions.

1. What triggers escalation?

Use observable conditions where possible:

  • assigned coach has not reached the staging point by the readiness deadline;
  • confirmed capacity is below the current passenger count;
  • guest requiring an accessible vehicle cannot be served by the assigned resource;
  • group is likely to miss a timed venue entry or onward connection;
  • client requests a material change after operational release;
  • an unverified person requests passenger information;
  • a supplier fails to respond after the stated attempts and interval;
  • injury, safeguarding concern, missing vulnerable guest, or credible threat is reported; or
  • the operating team loses access to a critical system or current manifest.

“When necessary” is not a trigger. Neither is “if serious,” unless seriousness is defined.

2. Who owns the first response?

The person who sees the exception needs immediate actions within their competence and authority. These may include protecting the guest, stopping an unsafe action, checking the current operating source, separating verified facts from assumptions, preserving contact, and notifying the control role.

The SOP should not ask frontline staff to wait passively when a safe, approved stabilizing action is available.

3. Who decides at each level?

Use roles, not personal names. A typical path might be:

  1. airport representative or driver;
  2. movement controller or dispatcher;
  3. duty operations manager;
  4. event lead or head of operations;
  5. designated incident, continuity, crisis, safety, security, or executive role.

The path may branch. A safety or safeguarding trigger may bypass normal commercial authority. A personal-data concern may require the privacy or information-security role. A client change may require commercial approval as well as operational feasibility.

4. How quickly must the role respond?

Set service-appropriate response expectations: immediate notification for protective issues, a defined acknowledgment time for live operational exceptions, and a decision or update interval where resolution takes longer.

Avoid setting arbitrary times in a generic corporate template. Response requirements should reflect consequence, speed of onset, guest exposure, programme dependency, contractual commitments, operating hours, and actual staffing.

5. What authority is available?

Define authority for actions such as:

  • delaying or releasing a movement;
  • substituting a vehicle, guide, hotel, attraction, or route;
  • buying an emergency service within a limit;
  • changing guest allocation;
  • offering approved service recovery;
  • informing the client;
  • suspending a supplier;
  • activating an offline process;
  • calling relevant emergency services; and
  • activating continuity or incident coordination.

Authority should include constraints. A manager may approve additional transport cost but not waive a safety, accessibility, immigration, insurance, or data-protection requirement.

6. What information must travel with the escalation?

A weak escalation transfers anxiety. A strong escalation transfers a decision-ready picture.

One concise briefing structure is FACT:

  • Facts: What is confirmed? What remains unverified?
  • Actions: What has already been done to stabilize or investigate?
  • Choices: Which safe, feasible options exist, and what authority or decision is required?
  • Time: When is the decision needed, and when will the next update be provided?

Example:

Facts: Coach C12 has a reported mechanical warning and remains at the staging area. Forty-two delegates are ready; the hotel journey normally takes approximately 35 minutes. Actions: driver has stopped movement, supplier control has been notified, guests remain with two hosts, and water is available. Choices: approve backup coach B07 with an estimated arrival of 18 minutes, or split the group across two confirmed vehicles with sufficient capacity. Decision required: authorize the selected replacement and related cost. Time: decision needed in five minutes to protect the programme; next update in ten minutes.

The exact times and options must be verified in the live operation. The structure prevents opinion from being presented as fact and gives the decision owner something actionable.

7. What happens if the assigned person cannot be reached?

Every live escalation path needs a fallback:

  • primary role and approved channel;
  • secondary role or duty number;
  • number of attempts and interval where appropriate;
  • next level if no acknowledgment occurs;
  • offline alternative if a system or channel fails; and
  • rule for immediate protective action.

A contact list without coverage hours, alternates, and maintenance ownership is not a reliable escalation system.

Write exception content inside the SOP

Exception control should not be hidden only in a separate emergency manual. The operating SOP needs enough information for the user to recognize and route the condition. It can then reference specialized controlled plans.

A useful exception section contains:

  1. the exception or trigger;
  2. immediate stabilizing action;
  3. restrictions or prohibited action;
  4. role to notify and required channel;
  5. information required;
  6. decision authority;
  7. response or update time;
  8. approved options or referenced contingency;
  9. guest/client communication owner;
  10. records required; and
  11. criteria for closure, handover, or plan activation.

The step sequence should distinguish what the employee shall do from what the decision owner may authorize.

Practical tool: the exception and escalation matrix

The following abbreviated matrix shows the design logic. Values are illustrative and must be approved for the actual operation.

TriggerImmediate actionEscalate toAuthority/decisionCommunicationEvidence/closure
Assigned vehicle late beyond readiness thresholdConfirm location and status; keep guests informed and supportedMovement controllerResequence within approved windowHost gives verified holding updateTime, reason, action, actual arrival
Capacity below confirmed demandStop loading that would exceed legal/approved capacity; verify countDuty operations managerApprove suitable additional or replacement resourceController updates event lead/client per thresholdManifest, vehicle assignment, approval, final count
Confirmed access need cannot be metProtect dignity and do not improvise an unsuitable transferDuty manager and accessibility/service ownerApprove compliant alternative and recoveryNamed guest-contact role communicates privatelyRequirement, actions, consent where relevant, outcome
Guest not locatedCheck approved meeting points and current status; maintain group controlAirport controllerExtend search, reallocate host, or classify no-show under approved ruleAuthorized role contacts guest/client using approved dataSearch log, contacts, decision, baggage/group impact
Injury or immediate threatFollow local emergency arrangements and protect peopleRelevant emergency services/authority and designated internal incident roleCompetent response takes priority; internal role coordinates supportOnly authorized spokesperson handles wider communicationIncident record, official references, actions, handover
Critical system unavailableSwitch to approved offline pack and verify latest controlled dataDuty manager/continuity roleContinue, restrict, or suspend affected processTargeted internal/client updateOutage time, dataset version, reconciliation, return-to-system check

The matrix should not become unreadable. High-complexity responses can reference a work instruction, contingency plan, contact directory, or role card.

A multi-exception MICE scenario

Consider an evening arrival wave with three flights and 160 delegates. One flight lands early. The first coach reports a warning light. Twelve delegates are not on the current printed manifest, and one traveller has a confirmed wheelchair-accessible transfer requirement. The hotel asks to move part of the group to a different entrance because another event is checking in.

Without a control model, each team member may solve a different problem. The airport host starts calling reservations. The driver asks the hotel for direction. The supplier dispatches a smaller vehicle. The client receives three conflicting updates. The printed manifest gains handwritten changes that never reach the movement controller.

With a controlled model:

  1. The representative verifies the current passenger data and separates unverified names from confirmed allocations.
  2. The driver follows the vehicle safety response; the coach is not released merely to protect timing.
  3. The movement controller establishes one operating picture and logs each exception.
  4. The accessible transfer remains protected as a specific service requirement, not traded away for general capacity.
  5. The duty manager decides replacement capacity and cost within the authority matrix.
  6. The hotel entrance change is verified, assessed for movement and accessibility effect, approved, and issued through the controlled change channel.
  7. The event lead receives one FACT briefing with impact, actions, options, decision needs, and next update.
  8. Hosts communicate only confirmed guest-facing information.
  9. Completion, unresolved issues, cost, and required follow-up are recorded before handover or closure.

The team does not need a separate escalation for every symptom if the issues are interdependent. The controller groups them into a coherent operating picture while maintaining ownership for each action.

This control-room approach is expanded in When the MICE Plan Changes, The Fleet Control Tower, and The Abu Dhabi MICE Movement Control Room.

Communication during exceptions

Good service communication is not an apology template added at the end. It is a controlled part of response.

The SOP should assign:

  • who communicates with the affected guest;
  • who updates the client or travel partner;
  • who coordinates with suppliers and venues;
  • who may communicate externally or publicly;
  • which facts are approved for release;
  • language, accessibility, privacy, and channel considerations;
  • update frequency when resolution is not immediate; and
  • how communications are recorded.

A useful guest update usually acknowledges the situation, states what is known without speculation, explains the action under way, gives a realistic next update, and provides a way to obtain help. It should not expose another guest’s information, assign blame before facts are established, or promise an outcome outside the communicator’s authority.

Technology can support prepared messages and faster status management, but human review and authority remain essential. The Guest Experience AI Toolkit discusses responsible support for guest communication.

Record the decision, not only the problem

An exception record should allow another authorized person to reconstruct:

  • date, time, service, location, and reference;
  • who identified and classified the exception;
  • verified facts and information sources;
  • people or services affected;
  • immediate actions;
  • notifications and acknowledgment times;
  • options considered;
  • decision, authority, rationale, and time;
  • communications issued;
  • recovery and completion status;
  • cost or contractual effect;
  • linked incident, complaint, supplier, or corrective-action record; and
  • closure owner and follow-up date.

Do not collect sensitive information merely because a form has space. Access, retention, and sharing should follow approved requirements.

An exception register is valuable because repeated “small” deviations may reveal a systemic issue: late supplier confirmation, unclear handover, poor master data, unworkable cutoff, or an SOP step that does not match reality.

Close, review, and learn

Operational closure is not the same as learning. The guest may have reached the hotel while cost, client response, supplier action, record reconciliation, or corrective work remains open.

Define closure criteria:

  • people are safe and the service is stable or formally handed over;
  • affected parties have received the required update;
  • operational records are complete;
  • temporary changes are reconciled into the source of truth;
  • costs and approvals are captured;
  • required reporting is initiated;
  • an owner and date exist for outstanding actions; and
  • the event is screened for review, trend, or corrective action.

Review depth should be proportionate. A routine deviation may need trend coding. A material incident may need a structured review that separates immediate cause, contributing conditions, control failure, and organizational learning. Avoid a search for the person to blame; examine why the system allowed the condition or failed to detect and recover from it.

ISO 22301:2019 provides requirements for business-continuity management systems, while ISO 22313:2020 offers guidance on applying them. Operational exception management should connect to, not compete with, the organization’s continuity arrangements. If a disruption crosses the approved activation threshold, the SOP should route the team to the relevant plan and governance.

Test the exception design

An escalation matrix that has never been exercised may fail under pressure. Test realistic scenarios through walkthroughs, tabletop exercises, simulations, or controlled drills.

Check whether participants can:

  • identify the trigger;
  • find the current document and contact path;
  • take safe immediate action;
  • distinguish fact from assumption;
  • reach an authorized role;
  • use the fallback when that role is unavailable;
  • produce a decision-ready briefing;
  • protect guest communication and information;
  • work offline where designed;
  • keep an adequate record; and
  • hand back to normal operations.

Exercises should test nights, weekends, supplier interfaces, and simultaneous events—not only office-hours scenarios with every manager present.

Common design failures

Escalate everything

If every minor variation goes to the general manager, the process is slow and management attention is diluted. Give competent roles clear tolerances and authority.

Escalate nothing until failure is visible

Late escalation removes options. Use leading triggers, such as unconfirmed capacity by a deadline, not only the final failure.

Create a long phone tree

A phone tree is not governance. Identify the decision owner, the backup, the required information, the response expectation, and the next level.

Focus only on cost

Tourism exceptions may affect safety, accessibility, dignity, privacy, programme, contract, trust, and staff welfare. Consider the full consequence.

Use uncontrolled messaging groups as the only record

Fast channels can support coordination, but the authoritative decision and required evidence must reach the controlled record.

Confuse service recovery with root-cause correction

An upgrade or apology may restore the guest relationship. It does not correct the process weakness that caused the issue.

The writing test

Before approving the SOP, select the five most credible operational exceptions and ask a trained person to use the document without coaching.

Can the person tell:

  • that the normal path has been exceeded;
  • what must happen immediately;
  • what must not happen;
  • who owns the next decision;
  • how to reach that role and the fallback;
  • what information to provide;
  • which options are within authority;
  • who communicates with the guest and client;
  • what must be recorded; and
  • how the operation is returned or handed over?

If the answer depends on “everyone knows,” the SOP is incomplete.

The structural foundation is covered in How to Write a Professional SOP: Part 1 — Structure. Together, structure and exception management turn the SOP from a description of ideal work into a practical operating control.

Key takeaway

Professional tourism operations do not eliminate every exception. They reduce preventable variation and make the remaining variation visible, owned, time-bound, authorized, communicated, evidenced, and learnable. The best escalation section is not the most dramatic. It is the one a competent employee can use calmly when the plan changes.

Sources and further reading

  • ISO 31000:2018 — Risk management — Guidelines
  • IEC 31010:2019 — Risk management — Risk assessment techniques
  • ISO 22301:2019 — Security and resilience — Business continuity management systems — Requirements
  • ISO 22313:2020 — Guidance on the use of ISO 22301
  • ISO 23592:2021 — Service excellence — Principles and model
  • ISO 21902:2021 — Tourism and related services — Accessible tourism for all

Editorial note: This article provides a professional operating-design framework, not legal, safety, emergency-response, accessibility, privacy, or regulatory advice. Organizations should validate procedures against applicable requirements, competent-authority guidance, contracts, insurance conditions, destination context, and their approved management systems.

description: Design records that capture timely, factual, proportionate evidence of what happened—without turning operational documentation into improvised legal conclusions.
html:
Design records that capture timely, factual, proportionate evidence of what happened—without turning operational documentation into improvised legal conclusions.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S14
Audience
Tourism operations managers, quality teams, duty managers, and SOP authors handling incidents, complaints, no-shows, and supplier disputes
Practical tool
Evidence architecture and factual operational log template
Running example
A disputed airport no-show involving flight data, calls, meeting-point checks, and supervisor decisions

The operating problem

Defensible operations begin with sound service design and contemporaneous facts. Records should show the source, time, action, decision, authority, communication, and outcome; they should not be reconstructed to support a preferred story. Tourism work makes this discipline unusually important. A single service may join Sales, Reservations, Operations, a hotel, an airport team, a transport partner, a guide, a client, and the guest. Information changes while the service is live, and the person who notices a problem may not hold the authority to change cost, timing, supplier, or customer promise. The document therefore has to work as an operating interface, not simply as well-written office content. The starting point is the broader system described in the operating-system overview. That system separates governance, execution, evidence, measurement, and improvement. The present article focuses on one controlled component, while the document-type comparison explains why an SOP, work instruction, checklist, form, template, and record should not be asked to perform the same job. This is a practical management model, not a universal template imposed by ISO or a substitute for applicable law, contract terms, safety requirements, privacy advice, or emergency arrangements. An organization should tailor the depth, approval, terminology, and retained evidence to its services, risk, size, jurisdiction, technology, and competence. Approval should therefore be evidence-led. Reviewers should see the mapped work, representative records, relevant risk and guest requirements, user-test observations, and unresolved issues—not only the polished draft. That evidence makes the approval decision explainable and gives the owner a baseline for measuring whether the released control improves real performance.

The distinctions that prevent document failure

A controlled blank form is documented information maintained for use. Once completed, the record is retained evidence. These need related but different controls for access, correction, retention, and disposal. A fact is directly observed or reliably captured: ‘flight status changed to landed at 18:42 on the approved feed’. An inference is a conclusion: ‘guest deliberately avoided the representative’. Records should identify the difference. Completeness does not mean collecting every possible data point. The organization should define a lawful operational purpose and minimize personal information to what is necessary for that purpose. Legal defensibility depends on jurisdiction, contract, sector rules, and professional advice. An SOP can support accurate records and governance; it cannot promise that a document will decide a dispute or replace counsel.

Practical tool: Evidence architecture and factual operational log template

The following canvas is designed for a working session, not decorative inclusion in a manual. Complete it using a real service and current records. Every answer should be specific enough for another role to validate.

ElementControl questionTourism example
IdentityWhich service and record is this?Job reference, form number, version
Time and sourceWhen and from where was information obtained?System timestamp, call log, named role
ObservationWhat fact was seen, heard, or received?Meeting-point check completed; guest not located
ActionWhat did the team do?Called contact, checked desk, informed supervisor
Decision and authorityWho decided what, under which rule?No-show declared by Duty Manager at threshold
OutcomeHow was the service closed and followed up?Client notified, vehicle released, case routed for review

The table is intentionally compact. Supporting detail should live in the appropriate controlled document or system rather than expanding one tool until it becomes impossible to use. During review, mark assumptions, unresolved authority, weak inputs, and missing evidence separately; do not convert them into confident statements merely to finish the template.

A professional design workflow

1. Define the evidence purpose

For each record, state which operational decision, handoff, customer commitment, compliance need, or improvement process it supports. Remove fields that have no defined use.

2. Specify source and timestamp rules

Decide which times come automatically from systems and which are entered by staff. State the time zone, format, and correction method, especially when teams and suppliers use different channels.

3. Use factual prompts

Prompts such as ‘location checked’, ‘contact method’, ‘response received’, and ‘decision authorized by’ produce better records than an empty box titled ‘explanation’.

4. Link actions to authority

A no-show, service cancellation, extra cost, or data disclosure should reference the approving role and applicable threshold. This makes later review possible without asking staff to write legal opinions.

5. Control attachments and messages

If screenshots, GPS data, email, call logs, or messaging exports are retained, define lawful use, access, naming, linkage, security, and retention. Do not assume that availability equals permission.

6. Protect corrections and closure

Permit genuine corrections through a traceable method that retains the original entry, reason, date, and person making the change. Define when the record is complete and who reviews exceptions. Ask users to work from the draft and approved tools without whispered instructions. Any dependency on a particular manager's memory should be recorded, owned, and resolved through the correct control—document, system, authority, contract, resource, or competence—before release.

Running example: A disputed airport no-show involving flight data, calls, meeting-point checks, and supervisor decisions

Initial record

The coordinator records the scheduled service, flight number, approved meeting point, assigned representative, and guest contact method from the current service order.

Live observations

System times, meeting-point checks, paging or desk inquiries, calls, and messages are logged as they occur. ‘No response’ is recorded separately from ‘number invalid’.

Decision point

At the approved threshold, the supervisor reviews the log and records the no-show decision, vehicle-release instruction, and any continued support.

Communication

The client receives a factual summary using the approved template. The record identifies what was communicated and when, without adding blame or speculation.

Review

If disputed, the company can reconstruct the timeline, identify gaps, and assess compliance with contract and procedure. Legal or commercial conclusions are handled by authorized specialists.

The scenario should be validated against the service's current risk assessment and guest journey, not treated as a perfect script. Compare it with the methods in operational risk assessment before SOP writing and customer journey mapping for SOP design. Those articles help the team check whether an internally neat design also addresses operational uncertainty and the guest's visible experience.

Common failure modes—and the design response

  • Backfilling precise times from memory. Use a recent case to show the operational consequence and identify the earliest control that could have prevented or detected it.
  • Editing an original entry without an audit trail. Trace the issue across roles and handoffs; the visible error may originate in an earlier input, authority decision, or system rule.
  • Copying sensitive guest data into uncontrolled chats. Decide whether the remedy belongs in this document, a supporting tool, the system, the contract, resource planning, or competence development.
  • Recording blame, emotion, or legal conclusions as fact. Test the proposed correction in a normal case and an exception so that solving one failure does not create another downstream.
  • Retaining everything forever ‘just in case’. Assign an owner and evidence for the correction, then set a date to confirm that the failure has not simply moved into an unofficial workaround.
  • Using screenshots without source, service reference, or context. Where risk remains, record and escalate it explicitly rather than adding vague cautionary prose that no user can apply under pressure.

Implementation and control

  1. Create an evidence schedule for every sop. Confirm the mandate, affected processes, and release decision so ownership does not disappear after the workshop.
  2. Review privacy and retention with authorized specialists. Schedule the work around live operations and include every shift, location, or partner needed to validate the design.
  3. Train staff using fact-versus-inference exercises. Keep an issue log with decision owner and due date; unresolved assumptions should never be disguised as approved instructions.
  4. Test access and retrieval during a mock dispute. Define the evidence of readiness—approved content, system access, supporting tools, briefed partners, competent users, and supervisor cover.
  5. Audit the quality of records rather than only their existence. Set an early-use review and a routine review trigger, then route defects, competence gaps, and resource problems to different actions.

Implementation should be staged. Begin with a representative service, observe use, and correct design defects before large-scale release. Control the approved version through document control and version management, and use training, competency, and SOP adoption to distinguish a distribution list from genuine competence and adoption.

Measures that show whether the control works

A useful measure should help the owner decide, not simply make a dashboard look complete. Establish a definition, data source, owner, review frequency, context, and action threshold for each selected measure.

Candidate measureWhat the owner should learn
Records complete at service closureWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Entries with traceable source and timeWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Corrections following the approved methodWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Cases retrieved within target timeWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome
Privacy or unauthorized-access exceptionsWhether the design is understood, usable, timely, and producing the intended operational evidence or outcome

A temporary increase in reported exceptions can be healthy after training if staff have begun recording issues that were previously hidden. Field review before approval

Boundary

Does the document begin and end at points the team can identify, or does it absorb adjacent processes until no owner can validate it? State the trigger, completion condition, excluded work, and connected processes. Then follow one real job reference from start to finish and note every point where the draft crosses its own boundary.

Roles and authority

Can every action and decision be traced to a current role, deputy, authority level, and escalation path across shifts and partners? Compare the draft with rosters, job descriptions, delegation limits, and partner contacts. Ask the night or weekend shift who actually decides when the named manager is unavailable.

Time and sequence

Are triggers, deadlines, intervals, pause points, and handoffs measurable in the systems and working conditions actually used? Use timestamps from a normal case and a disrupted case. Replace vague timing with an observable event or controlled threshold, and confirm that the relevant system or record can capture it.

Information quality

Are required inputs current, traceable, appropriately protected, and presented in a form that the receiving role can use without reinterpretation? Trace each critical value to its source, owner, format, and latest valid version. Resolve duplicate fields and define what the receiver does when two approved-looking sources disagree.

Exceptions

Has the team tested delay, absence, conflicting information, technology failure, supplier failure, accessibility needs, and a changing guest situation? Run at least one scenario that exceeds front-line authority. Observe whether staff can recognize the trigger, stabilize the service, escalate with the right facts, communicate, and return the case to controlled closure.

Evidence

Does the record capture timely facts, source, action, authority, and outcome without unnecessary personal data, speculation, or retrospective reconstruction? Reconstruct a recent event using only retained records. Missing links reveal where the design needs a prompt, automatic timestamp, approval trace, attachment rule, or clearer close-out responsibility.

Guest experience

Does the control protect the guest's clarity, dignity, accessibility, time, and communication needs as well as the company's internal workflow? Walk through what the guest sees, hears, waits for, and must do. Check language, channel, physical access, assistance, uncertainty, and recovery rather than assuming internal compliance equals a good experience.

Usability

Can representative users perform the work on the actual device or paper format, under interruption and time pressure, without unofficial notes? Watch rather than coach. Record where users pause, scroll, search, abbreviate, take screenshots, or switch to personal tools; those behaviors are design evidence, not merely user resistance.

Partner interface

Do external providers understand the same requirement, status, contact, evidence, and change rules, including the right to raise a concern early? Ask the partner to explain the handoff in their own words and demonstrate the communication route. Resolve differences before release, especially around substitutions, delay, cost, guest contact, and retained evidence.

Learning and review

Will operational data, user feedback, complaints, audits, and change triggers lead to a controlled revision rather than a parallel workaround? Name who reviews which signals, how often, and what action threshold applies. Connect urgent correction, routine revision, refresher training, supplier action, and formal improvement to distinct governance routes.

A reader should be able to follow the series from system design to live use and improvement without encountering a forced link in every paragraph. Those pieces provide concrete examples of journeys, dashboards, assignments, quality tools, commercial controls, partner handoffs, or service recovery. This article extends them by explaining the management method behind reliable execution.

  • The purpose, boundary, users, owner, and approval authority are explicit.

  • Supporting SOPs, work instructions, checklists, forms, templates, records, and training do not contradict one another.

Tourism Operations Excellence Series · Article S16
Audience
Tourism supervisors, dispatch teams, guides, transport coordinators, quality teams, and SOP authors
Practical tool
Read–Do and Do–Confirm checklist design canvas
Running example
A pre-departure coach checklist for a multi-hotel MICE movement

The operating problem

A checklist is a focused cognitive aid for critical actions or confirmations. It should not reproduce the full SOP, substitute for competence, or become a ceremonial sign-off completed after the work. Tourism work makes this discipline unusually important. A single service may join Sales, Reservations, Operations, a hotel, an airport team, a transport partner, a guide, a client, and the guest. Information changes while the service is live, and the person who notices a problem may not hold the authority to change cost, timing, supplier, or customer promise. The document therefore has to work as an operating interface, not simply as well-written office content. The starting point is the broader system described in the operating-system overview. That system separates governance, execution, evidence, measurement, and improvement. The present article focuses on one controlled component, while the document-type comparison explains why an SOP, work instruction, checklist, form, template, and record should not be asked to perform the same job. This is a practical management model, not a universal template imposed by ISO or a substitute for applicable law, contract terms, safety requirements, privacy advice, or emergency arrangements. An organization should tailor the depth, approval, terminology, and retained evidence to its services, risk, size, jurisdiction, technology, and competence. Approval should therefore be evidence-led. Reviewers should see the mapped work, representative records, relevant risk and guest requirements, user-test observations, and unresolved issues—not only the polished draft. That evidence makes the approval decision explainable and gives the owner a baseline for measuring whether the released control improves real performance.

The distinctions that prevent document failure

In a Read–Do checklist, the user reads an item and performs it before moving on. It suits unfamiliar, tightly sequenced, or infrequent work. In a Do–Confirm checklist, trained staff perform a familiar flow and pause to verify critical items. A checklist item should be observable: ‘coach bay confirmed with venue’ is testable; ‘ensure smooth departure’ is not. The item can point to a work instruction when technical detail is required. Yes/No/N/A can support review only when N/A is legitimately defined and ‘No’ opens an action path. Otherwise the response format encourages box-ticking instead of control. Completion evidence should be proportionate to risk. The company may need named sign-off for a safety-critical or commercial release, but not a timestamp for every routine mental check.

Practical tool: Read–Do and Do–Confirm checklist design canvas

The following canvas is designed for a working session, not decorative inclusion in a manual. Complete it using a real service and current records. Every answer should be specific enough for another role to validate.

ElementControl questionTourism example
Pause pointWhen is attention deliberately focused?Before dispatch, before loading, before departure
Critical itemWhat omission would materially affect service?Correct coach, route, guest count, accessibility, contact
Observable wordingWhat can the user confirm?Vehicle registration matches movement brief
ResponseHow is status shown?Done, No, N/A with reason
ExceptionWhat happens when the check fails?Stop, correct, notify, or escalate
EvidenceWhat completion record is proportionate?Named digital confirmation at the pause point

The table is intentionally compact. Supporting detail should live in the appropriate controlled document or system rather than expanding one tool until it becomes impossible to use. During review, mark assumptions, unresolved authority, weak inputs, and missing evidence separately; do not convert them into confident statements merely to finish the template.

A professional design workflow

1. Select a specific pause point

Avoid a single checklist covering an entire shift. Place a short aid where a team can realistically stop: vehicle release, guest loading, attraction departure, or service close-out.

2. Identify critical omissions

Use process maps, risk assessments, complaints, and field observation to find items whose omission is plausible and consequential. Do not include every good practice simply because it is true.

3. Choose Read–Do or Do–Confirm

Match the mode to familiarity, sequence, time pressure, and consequence. Label the mode in training so users understand whether the list directs the task or verifies a completed flow.

4. Write short observable items

Use one idea per line, familiar operational language, and the value to be checked. If an item requires a paragraph, move the method into the SOP or work instruction.

5. Design the exception response

For each ‘No’, define whether the user corrects the issue, stops release, contacts a role, or records an authorized deviation. A checklist without a failure path only detects problems.

6. Test under pressure

Observe use during a realistic service with interruptions, gloves, low light, noisy bays, mobile screens, and language needs where relevant. Revise based on skipped items and user explanations. After completing the workflow, test the connected design during a pre-departure coach checklist for a multi-hotel mice movement. Ask users to work from the draft and approved tools without whispered instructions. Running example: A pre-departure coach checklist for a multi-hotel MICE movement

Readiness pause

Thirty minutes before the first hotel departure, the controller confirms coach registration, driver contact, access, route, signage, water, mobility arrangements, and guide assignment.

Loading pause

The guide performs the normal loading flow and uses a Do–Confirm list for hotel, movement code, guest count, baggage or equipment status, and missing-person escalation.

Failed check

A registration mismatch is marked ‘No’. The list directs the controller to stop release, compare the approved assignment, contact Dispatch, and record the corrected vehicle.

N/A control

A mobility-equipment check can be N/A only when the current guest/service brief confirms no requirement; the rationale is captured without disclosing unnecessary health information.

After action

Supervisors review failed checks and repeated N/A use. The data identifies weak inputs or supplier performance rather than rewarding perfect-looking sheets.

  5. Review checklist value after incidents and operational changes. Set an early-use review and a routine review trigger, then route defects, competence gaps, and resource problems to different actions.

3. Write the message architecture

4. Design variables safely

Use clearly marked fields with source and validation rules. Prevent blank placeholders, wrong names, old times, internal codes, or hidden instructions from reaching the recipient.

5. Adapt by channel and audience

6. Test normal and stressed use

7. Control and learn
